title: Use of `payable.transfer()` Might Render ETH Impossible to Withdraw
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L105
https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L85-L86
https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L109
https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/OpenEdition.sol#L92


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The protocol uses Solidity’s `transfer()` when transferring ETH to the recipients. This has some notable shortcomings when the recipient is a smart contract, which can render ETH impossible to transfer. Specifically, the transfer will inevitably fail when the smart contract:

- does not implement a payable fallback function, or
- implements a payable fallback function which would incur more than 2300 gas units, or
- implements a payable fallback function incurring less than 2300 gas units but is called through a proxy that raises the call’s gas usage above 2300.

## Proof of Concept
[File: LPDA.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol)

```
85:            ISaleFactory(factory).feeReceiver().transfer(fee);
86:            temp.saleReceiver.transfer(totalSale - fee);

105:        payable(msg.sender).transfer(owed);
```
[File: FixedPrice.sol#L109](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L109)

```
109:        ISaleFactory(factory).feeReceiver().transfer(address(this).balance / 20);
```
[File: OpenEdition.sol#L92](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/OpenEdition.sol#L92)

```
92:        ISaleFactory(factory).feeReceiver().transfer(address(this).balance / 20);
```
Issues pertaining to the use of `transfer()` in the code blocks above may be referenced further via:

- [CONSENSYS Diligence's article](https://consensys.net/diligence/blog/2019/09/stop-using-soliditys-transfer-now/)
- [OpenZeppelin news & events](https://blog.openzeppelin.com/reentrancy-after-istanbul/)
 
## Tools Used
Manual inspection

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Using `call` with its returned boolean checked in combination with re-entrancy guard is highly recommended after December 2019.

For instance, [line 105](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L105) in `LPDA.sol` may be refactored as follows:

```
- payable(msg.sender).transfer(owed);
+ (bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{ value: owed }('');
+ require(success, " Transfer of ETH Failed");
```
Alternatively, `Address.sendValue()` available in [OpenZeppelin Contract’s Address library](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/utils/Address.sol#L44-L65) can be used to transfer the Ether without being limited to 2300 gas units. 

And again, in either of the above measures adopted, the risks of re-entrancy stemming from the use of this function can be mitigated by tightly following the “Check-effects-interactions” pattern and/or using [OpenZeppelin Contract’s ReentrancyGuard contract](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/security/ReentrancyGuard.sol#L43-L54).

title: LPDA refund() function can lock user refunds if they submitted from a smart contract
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L105


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In LPDA.sol, the `refund()` function calculates the difference between what a user spent in the auction and their actual cost (calculated as final price * amount). It then refunds the difference to the user.

This refund is performed with a `.transfer` call that doesn't allow the user to specify the address. In the event that the original transactions came from a smart contract that uses more than 2300 gas in its `receive()` or `fallback()` function, the refund will revert and the user will not be able to access their fees.

## Proof of Concept
- User calls `buy()` with 50 ETH for 5 NFTs, expecting to get a refund
- `receipts[msg.sender]` is set with their quantity and balance
- The final NFT sells for 5 ETH
- The user's refund should (10-5) * 5 = 25 ETH
- If the user's initial transaction came from a smart contract that can't receive ETH without using more than 2300 gas, the `.transfer` call will fail
- The user will have no alternative way to access their funds, because they are only able to withdraw them to this contract address, which is immutable

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Two options:
1) Allow a `to` input to the `refund()` function, which would allow users to send their refund to another address if they aren't able to accept it.
2) Use a low level call to send the refund, so that the hard gas cap doesn't apply.

title: saleReceiver with logic in receive() or fallback() function will lead to funds permanently stuck in LPDA contract
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L85-L86


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Using `.transfer` to transfer ETH only sends 2300 gas along with the call.

If a creator selects a `saleReceiver` that is a contract with any logic in the `receive()` or `fallback()` functions, this transfer is likely to run out of gas and revert.

Since the `saleReceiver` is not changeable once the contract is deployed, the result is that all the funds from the mint could get stuck in the contract and will be permanently unclaimable, including protocol fees.

https://consensys.net/diligence/blog/2019/09/stop-using-soliditys-transfer-now/

https://blog.openzeppelin.com/opyn-gamma-protocol-audit/

## Proof of Concept

While the FixedPrice and OpenEdition contracts use `selfdestruct()` to send ETH to the `saleReceiver`, the LPDA.sol contract uses `.transfer`. 

This `.transfer` is called when the final NFT is minted (so that `newId == temp.finalId`). There is no other place in the contract where the balance of the contract can be distributed.

As a result, if the `saleReceiver` address is set to one where receiving ETH uses more than 2300 gas, the final NFT mint will revert, and the creator will never be able to redeem the money from the contract.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Use a low level call to allow for more gas to be used for this specific transfer.

title: Unsafe downcasting to set sale.finalPrice in LPDAs
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L82


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
After an LPDA auction is ended, the final price is locked in as follows:

```solidity
sale.finalPrice = uint80(price);
```

This unsafe downcasting casts price into an 80 bit integer. This may be sufficient for most situations, but only represents 1.208MM ETH, which is not out of the question for how much an NFT might one day sell for.

## Proof of Concept
If an NFT were to sell for 1.209MM ETH:
- `price = 1209 * 10 ** 18;`
- `sale.finalPrice = uint80(price);`
- because of the unsafe downcasting, this value overflows to 74 ETH
- refund values are set based on this finalPrice, which is inaccurate

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Use safe downcasting by checking that the value of price is less than the max uint80 value before downcasting:

```solidity
require(price <= type(uint80).max, "CANT DOWNCAST");
```

This option would stop any NFTs from being purchased above this price. A simplier solution might be to rearrange the storage struct so that `finalPrice` is sized at uin96, which would fit within the existing slot and not cost any extra gas.

title: Creators of LPDA auctions cannot withdraw funds if auction doesn't sell out at final price
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L81-L88


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In an LPDA auction, the price falls from `startPrice` down to `startPrice - (dropPerSecond * (endTime - startTime)`. At this point, the auction continues, but the price no longer falls.

If the auction stops at a price that doesn't clear the market, it'll remain open indefinitely. 

But, as long as the auction remains open, the owners are not able to withdraw their funds and the feeReceiver doesn't receive their fees.

The result is that an NFT collection can be mostly minted and active, but the owners are not able to collect their earnings to fund the project.

## Proof of Concept
The only place in the LPDA.sol contract where funds are transferred to the `feeReceiver` and `saleReceiver` are in the final block of the `buy()` function:

```solidity
if (newId == temp.finalId) {
    sale.finalPrice = uint80(price);
    uint256 totalSale = price * amountSold;
    uint256 fee = totalSale / 20;
    ISaleFactory(factory).feeReceiver().transfer(fee);
    temp.saleReceiver.transfer(totalSale - fee);
    _end();
}
```

For this block to execute, the NFTs need to be minted up to the point where `newId == sale.finalId`. If this doesn't happen, this block can never execute.

There are only two ways for this to happen:

1) `cancel()` is called, which can only happen before a sale starts.
2) Enough NFTs are minted that currentId increases to the point that currentId + amount reaches finalId.

If the latter doesn't happen, the funds will be stuck.

[Note that this doesn't impact refunds, as users will be able to call `refund()` at any time to get their refund up to the current price.]

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add an `end()` function that can be called after the `endTime` to finalize the LPDA and process the payouts.

title: tokenURI function not included in Generative.sol
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/uris/Generative.sol#L1-L31


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Generative.sol is intended to create generative URIs. It sets a seed base and scripts, but doesn't implement any `tokenURI()` function to display the output. All of its functions and storage are unused.

As a result, it's `tokenURI()` function returns the simple concatenation that it inherits from Unique.sol.

## Proof of Concept
There is no `tokenURI()` function in Generative.sol. 

Because the contract inherits from Unique.sol, its `tokenURI()` function is as follows:

```solidity
function tokenURI(uint256 _tokenId) external view virtual override returns (string memory) {
    return string.concat(baseURI, _tokenId.toString());
}
```

This function doesn't use any of the functionality built in Generative.sol, and renders the rest of the contract useless.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add a `tokenURI()` function to Generative.sol:

```solidity
function tokenURI(uint256 _tokenId) external view virtual override returns (string memory) {
    return string.concat(baseURI, tokenToSeed(_tokenId));
}
```

title: Royalty functionality described in docs does not exist
description:

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The documentation describes the ability to set the royalties on a token-by-token basis using the `setTokenRoyalty` function. However, this function doesn't exist in the contract.

## Proof of Concept

In the docs, it explains that the flow for setting up a sale includes:

However, this function does not exist. While the inherited ERC2981.sol file does have a `_setTokenRoyalty()` internal function, Escher has not implemented any external function to access it.

Instead, it implements a `setDefaultRoyalty()` function, which doesn't have the same granularity laid out in the docs. 

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L85-L87
https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L105
https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L109
https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/OpenEdition.sol#L92


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Transfer function may revert and may stuck funds in the 3 minter smartcontracts 

Transfer will reverts, amongst other reasons, if the `to` address is a smarcontract not accepting payments

## Proof of Concept
Problem is low risk for FixedPrice [FixedPrice.sol#L109](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L109) and OpenEdition [OpenEdition.sol#L92](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/OpenEdition.sol#L92) contracts :
```solidity
ISaleFactory(factory).feeReceiver().transfer(address(this).balance / 20);
```
Because only transfer to feeReceiver address may reverts, and as this feeReceiver address can be changed by owner of the corresponding factory, the problem can be fixed this way.

Problem is higher for LPDA, because transfer also occurs (before _end) on saleReceiver [LPDA.sol#L86-L87](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L86-L87) :
```solidity
temp.saleReceiver.transfer(totalSale - fee);
_end();
```
That `saleReceiver` address can no more be modified, so if transfer fails, ending the sale becomes impossible.
Risky transfer may also occurs on refund. 
So funds could be lost forever, stuck in the contract.

On LPDA there is also these lower risk transfers [LPDA.sol#L85](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L85) :
```solidity
ISaleFactory(factory).feeReceiver().transfer(fee);
```
and [LPDA.sol#L105](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L105) :
```solidity
payable(msg.sender).transfer(owed);
```


## Tools Used
Manual inspection

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To avoid this transfer problems, you have to take into account the cases when the transfer reverts : so either catch the transfer revert with some  try/catch , or use call with value that returns a success boolean that can be tested

For exemple , replace :
```solidity
temp.saleReceiver.transfer(totalSale - fee);
```
with this call, that can't reverts : 
```solidity
(bool success,) = temp.saleReceiver.call{value: totalSale - fee: 2300 }("");
``` 
then do some logic if success is true or not

An additional function , allowing redrawing of funds from the contract can also be done.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
**Note**: While the code that is referenced here is also mentioned in the automated findings of this contest, the automation tool has mistakenly recognized these instances as ERC20 operations. So I outline in this report that these are not ERC20 operations and I will give a correct estimation of the impact.

The `transfer` function allows the callee to spend only 2300 Gas. This was introduced in order to mitigate Reentrancy attacks.  

However using the `transfer` function introduces issues for two reasons:
1. Function call reverts if callee runs code upon receiving ETH that uses more than 2300 Gas
2. Gas costs may change significantly in the future so using `transfer` may break code that runs successfully now

For the two reasons stated above, it must be assumed that calling the `transfer` function can fail which leads to DOS in the affected contracts.

Instances where `transfer` is used:  
[https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L109](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L109)  

[https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L85](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L85)  

[https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L86](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L86)  

[https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L105](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L105)  

[https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/OpenEdition.sol#L92](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/OpenEdition.sol#L92)  

## Proof of Concept
I will show the impact for the first instance of this issue ([https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L109](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L109)):  

If the `feeReceiver` employs code upon receiving ETH that uses up more than 2300 Gas, the call to the `FixedPrice._end` function will revert.  

This means the last NFT cannot be minted, the `feeReceiver` cannot receive fees and the `saleReceiver` cannot receive the revenue generated by selling NFTs.  

## Tools Used
VSCode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use `call()` instead of `transfer()`, and be sure to respect the CEI pattern and/or add re-entrancy guards to the functions that make use of `call()`.

Fix (for first instance):
```solidity
(bool success, ) = ISaleFactory(factory).feeReceiver().call{value: address(this).balance / 20}("");
require(success, "Transfer Failed");
```

title: Escher721 contract does not have setTokenRoyalty function
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/Escher721.sol#L10-L99


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
On the code4rena page of this contest there is a "SALES PATTERNS" section that describes the flow of how to use Sales:  

[https://code4rena.com/contests/2022-12-escher-contest](https://code4rena.com/contests/2022-12-escher-contest)  

It contains this statement:  
> If the artist would like sales and royalties to go somewhere other than the default royalty receiver, they  
> must call setTokenRoyalty with the following variables

So an artist should be able to call the `setTokenRoyalty` function on the `Escher721` contract.  

However this function cannot be called. It does not exist. There exists a `_setTokenRoyalty` in `ERC2981.sol` from openzeppelin. This function however is `internal` ([https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/3d7a93876a2e5e1d7fe29b5a0e96e222afdc4cfa/contracts/token/common/ERC2981.sol#L94](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/3d7a93876a2e5e1d7fe29b5a0e96e222afdc4cfa/contracts/token/common/ERC2981.sol#L94)).  

So there is no `setTokenRoyalty` function that can be called by the artist. So an artist cannot set a royalty individually for a token as is stated in the documentation.  

## Proof of Concept
I tried calling `setTokenRoyalty` from inside `Escher721.t.sol` with the following test:  
```solidity
function test_setDefaultRoyalty() public {
    edition.setTokenRoyalty(1,address(this), 5);
}
```
This won't even compile because the `setTokenRoyalty` function does not exist.  

## Tools Used
VSCode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
In order to expose the internal `_setTokenRoyalty` function to the artist, add the following function to the `Escher721` contract:  

```solidity
function setTokenRoyalty(
    uint256 tokenId,
    address receiver,
    uint96 feeNumerator
) public onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE) {
    _setTokenRoyalty(tokenId,receiver,feeNumerator);
}
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/OpenEdition.sol#L67


# Vulnerability details

## M-1 call() should be used instead of transfer() 

## Impact

Note: C4 declared this finding as an unsafe ERC20 operation in the c4udit output, which is not true (The Escher protocol does not support erc20 tokens). This is a deprecated ```transfer()``` that could significantly damage the protocol and the users.

If ```saleReceiver``` and ```feeReceiver``` where smart contracts and one of the scenarios described in the POC occurred, neither of them will be able to withdraw their funds, and they (funds) will be frozen in the contract, resulting in a loss of funds for both users and the protocol.

## Proof of Concept

The use of the deprecated ```transfer()``` function for a payable address will certainly make the transaction fail when:

- The claimer smart contract does not implement a payable fallback function.

- The claimer smart contract does implement a payable fallback which uses more than 2300 gas unit.

- The claimer smart contract implements a payable fallback function that needs less than 2300 gas units but is called through proxy, raising the call's gas usage above 2300.

- Some multisig wallets might also require higher gas than 2300.

A more detailed explanation can be found [here](https://consensys.net/diligence/blog/2019/09/stop-using-soliditys-transfer-now/).

Lines of code:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L85-L86

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L105

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider using .call() instead with the CEI pattern implemented correctly. .

```solidity
        (bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{value: owed}("");
        require(success, "Call failed");
```

```solidity
        (bool success, ) = ISaleFactory(factory).feeReceiver().call{value: address(this).balance / 20}("");
        require(success, "Call failed");  
```

## M-2 Use safeMint instead of mint for ERC721

## Impact
Users could lost their NFTs.

The ```msg.sender``` will be minted an nft when [buy](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L57-L67) is called.

However, if msg.sender is a contract address that does not support ERC721, the NFT can be frozen in the contract forever.

As per the documentation of EIP-721:

A wallet/broker/auction application MUST implement the wallet interface if it will accept safe transfers.

Ref: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-721

As per the documentation of ERC721.sol by Openzeppelin:

Ref: https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721.sol#L274-L285

## Proof of Concept

Lines of code:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L66

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L74

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/OpenEdition.sol#L67

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use [safeMint](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721.sol#L262-L272) instead of ```mint``` to check received address support for ERC721 implementation.

```solidity
    function _safeMint(
        address to,
        uint256 tokenId,
        bytes memory data
    ) internal virtual {
        _mint(to, tokenId);
        require(
            _checkOnERC721Received(address(0), to, tokenId, data),
            "ERC721: transfer to non ERC721Receiver implementer"
        );
    }
```

title: Unsafe cast in LPDA.buy can decrease paid amount by user
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L71


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In case if payment of user were more than uint80.max value, then the balance stored to receipt will be truncated to uint80.max. As result user will not be able to refund all that he overpaid.

## Proof of Concept
When user wants to buy tokens he calls LPDA.buy and provides ether with function.
Later the amount that he paid [is stored](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L71) in the receipt. It will be used when the price will decrease and user will be able to refund overpaid tokens.

The problem is that msg.value here is unsafely casted to uint80. That means that if user paid more than uint80.max value, then delta amount is lost as it's not stored into receipts[msg.sender].balance.
`receipts[msg.sender].balance += uint80(msg.value);`

So later he will not be able to withdraw all overpaid amount using refund as it uses [his balance](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L102).
## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
When casting check that msg.value is less than uint80.max

title: User Fund May Lose His Fund
USE A SAFE TRANSFER HELPER LIBRARY FOR ERC20 TRANSFERS
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L85
https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/OpenEdition.sol#L92
https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/5d8be6aa0e8634fdb2f328b99076b0d05fefab73/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L109


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In _end(), finalize() and buy() calls SaleFactory#transfer directly. There are two issues with using this contract directly:

SaleFactory#transfer function does not check the return value of these calls. Tokens that return false rather than revert to indicate failed transfers may silently fail rather than reverting as expected.
Since the SaleFactory contract require a boolean return value, attempting to transfer tokens with missing return values will revert.

SaleFactory payment terminal may issue project token to users even though their incoming token transfer failed.


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use a safe transfer library like OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 to ensure consistent handling of ERC20 return values and abstract over inconsistent ERC20 implementations.

Additionally, since payment terminals are meant to support a variety of ERC20s, consider writing simulation tests that make token transfers using payment terminals for the most popular and most unusual ERC20s.

title: Minters use `transfer` to send Ether, which assumes gas costs are constant
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/FixedPrice.sol#L109
https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L85
https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/LPDA.sol#L105
https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-escher/blob/main/src/minters/OpenEdition.sol#L92


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Minters use `transfer` to send Ether, which assumes gas costs are constant. 
This is not true, as gas costs are not constant. They have changed in the past and might change again in the future, and smart contracts should be robust to this fact. Solidity’s `transfer()` and `send()` use a hardcoded gas amount, so these methods should be avoided. 

## Proof of Concept

A hardfork happens and changes the gas costs of some EVM operations. As a result, the function `FixedPrice._end` stops working and users are unable to withdraw their funds.

## Tools Used

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/utilities/FeeWrapper.sol#L8


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The FeeWrapper contract can be used to wrap calls to arbitrary contracts to include a fee for a third party. The contract at a high level works as follows:

1. User calculates fee for amount
2. User calls FeeWrapper with the proper params and amounts (total and fee)
3. FeeWrapper takes funds from user
4. FeeWrapper sends fee amount to fee recipient
5. FeeWrapper calls the target contract, forwarding the amount. In the case of an ERC20 it approves the spend, in case of ETH it sends the value as call value.

The general approach sounds ok, however there is an important detail that will conflict with most contract implementations. In point 5 the caller to the target is the FeeWrapper itself, not the original user. This means that in the context of the target contract, `msg.sender` is the FeeWrapper contract. Most smart contract implementations will use the caller of the function as the beneficiary of the actions. For example, a swap action in a decentralized exchange will return the swapped assets back to the caller. A deposit on a lending protocol will associate the collateral with the caller of the function, and only the caller will be able to eventually redeem that collateral.

The potential impact of the issue will depend on the case, but it certainly can be high for many cases. We will explore a few situations of loss of funds for the `RubiconRouter` contract in the next section.

## Proof of Concept

There are many functions present in the `RubiconRouter` that utilize the `msg.sender`. In this section we will explore just two to demonstrate the issue. The first one is the `maxBuyAllAmount` function:

https://github.com/RubiconDeFi/rubi-protocol-v2/blob/master/contracts/utilities/RubiconRouter.sol#L338-L356

```solidity
338:     function maxBuyAllAmount(
339:         ERC20 buy_gem,
340:         ERC20 pay_gem,
341:         uint256 max_fill_amount
342:     ) external returns (uint256 fill) {
343:         //swaps msg.sender's entire balance in the trade
344:         uint256 maxAmount = _calcAmountAfterFee(
345:             ERC20(buy_gem).balanceOf(msg.sender)
346:         );
347: 
348:         IERC20(buy_gem).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), maxAmount);
349:         fill = RubiconMarket(RubiconMarketAddress).buyAllAmount(
350:             buy_gem,
351:             maxAmount,
352:             pay_gem,
353:             max_fill_amount
354:         );
355:         ERC20(buy_gem).transfer(msg.sender, fill);
356:     }
```

As we can see in the code snippet, the function will execute the action using the RubiconMarket and transfer the output amount back to the caller (line 355). In the context of the FeeWrapper call, the resulting amount will be sent to the FeeWrapper contract itself and not the original caller, which will cause a loss of funds.

The other case is the `offerWithETH` function:

https://github.com/RubiconDeFi/rubi-protocol-v2/blob/master/contracts/utilities/RubiconRouter.sol#L503-L545

```solidity
503:     function offerWithETH(
504:         uint256 pay_amt, //maker (ask) sell how much
505:         // ERC20 nativeETH, //maker (ask) sell which token
506:         uint256 buy_amt, //maker (ask) buy how much
507:         ERC20 buy_gem, //maker (ask) buy which token
508:         uint256 pos, //position to insert offer, 0 should be used if unknown
509:         address recipient // the recipient of the fill
510:     ) external payable returns (uint256) {
511:         require(
512:             msg.value == pay_amt,
513:             "didnt send enough native ETH for WETH offer"
514:         );
515: 
516:         uint256 _before = ERC20(buy_gem).balanceOf(address(this));
517: 
518:         IWETH(wethAddress).deposit{value: pay_amt}();
519: 
520:         if (
521:             IWETH(wethAddress).allowance(address(this), RubiconMarketAddress) <
522:             pay_amt
523:         ) {
524:             approveAssetOnMarket(wethAddress);
525:         }
526:         uint256 id = RubiconMarket(RubiconMarketAddress).offer(
527:             pay_amt,
528:             ERC20(wethAddress),
529:             buy_amt,
530:             buy_gem,
531:             pos,
532:             address(this), // router is owner of the offer
533:             recipient
534:         );
535: 
536:         // Track the user's order so they can cancel it
537:         userNativeAssetOrders[msg.sender].push(id);
538: 
539:         uint256 _after = ERC20(buy_gem).balanceOf(address(this));
540:         if (_after > _before) {
541:             //return any potential fill amount on the offer
542:             IERC20(buy_gem).safeTransfer(recipient, _after - _before);
543:         }
544:         return id;
545:     }
```

This function will create the offer in the RubiconMarket contract, and associate the offer id to the `msg.sender` on line 537. Again, in the context of the FeeWrapper usage, the caller will be the FeeWrapper itself and not the original caller. The offer will be associated with the FeeWrapper, which means the user won't be able to eventually manage it, causing loss of funds.

## Recommendation

It is difficult to propose a solution given the current architecture and how the RubiconRouter already works in relation to the use of `msg.sender` (or basically any smart contract thinking of the general case). The usual approach in these cases is to use meta-transactions, in which a trusted forwarder encodes the original caller in the calldata payload, while the target contract decodes this value and uses it as the `msg.sender` if the transaction is coming from the trusted forwarder. The OpenZeppelin contracts library includes support for this, but this would require fundamental changes to the target contract being used.

Another approach would be to add multicall features to the FeeWrapper contract. It would then be possible to execute multiple actions, and for example use a first action to execute the wrapped call and a second action to transfer the assets or ownership back to the original caller. This may not work for all cases, and it would still require extreme care to correctly prepare the actions and avoid any potential pitfall in the process.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A user may get sandwiched when opening a position. This results in worse prices for him and worsens the experience on the Rubicon platform.   

## Proof of Concept
We calculate both the `buy_amt` and the `max_fill_amount` for on-chain. This allows attackers to sandwich these traders. 

```solidity
buyAllAmount(ERC20 buy_gem, uint256 buy_amt, ERC20 pay_gem, uint256 max_fill_amount)
```


```solidity
uint256 _buyAmount = rubiconMarket.getBuyAmount(
    ERC20(_asset),
    ERC20(_quote),
    _maxFill.sub(_fee)
);

rubiconMarket.buyAllAmount(
    ERC20(_asset),
    _buyAmount,
    ERC20(_quote),
    _maxFill
);
```
Since neither the amount entered nor the amount returned is checked for soundness, an attacker can arbitrarily change the market conditions before the trade to degrade the users` expected leverage.
This results in users paying much more than they expected to receive the desired amount of `_minFill` tokens. This may result in them having much higher leverage than expected and being liquidated.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

We should either 1) calculate one of the two parameters off-chain and then pass it to the function, or 2) compare the values with an oracle price and revert if the two values differ too much.
1) has some implementation problems, since a user would have to calculate all the minimum amounts along the path. A more technical sound solution it to predict an acceptable *realized* leverage value.
2) is a technically simpler solution, but would only put an upper limit on the MEV that can be extracted from the user.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

**Due to trust in the Rubicon team, the external contract approves the maximum value to FeeWrapper before calling `rubicalls`, and not revoke approval after the interaction**. Then, the attacker can call `rubicalls` with carefully constructed parameters that encode `erc20.transferFrom(external, attack, amount)`, resulting in the external contract's token being stolen.

## Proof of Concept

Before the external contract interacts with the Rubicon contract by `rubicalls`, the token must be approved to FeeWrapper. The external contract **approves the maximum value of a certain token** to FeeWrapper, and **the approval of this token is not revoked** after the interaction. Then the attacker can steal the token of the external contract through the following code:

```solidity
/*
        token:  valuable token
        victim: external contract
        to:     attacker's address
        amount: token amount
    */
    function fun(address token, address victim, address to, uint256 amount) {
        FeeWrapper.FeeParams memory feeParams = FeeWrapper.FeeParams(
            fakeToken,  //contract deployed by attacker
            10e18,
            1e18, 
            victim
        );
        FeeWrapper.CallParams memory params = FeeWrapper.CallParams(
            ERC20.transferFrom.selector,
            abi.encode(victim, to, route, amount),
            token,
            feeParams
        );
        FeeWrapper(feeWrapper).rubicall(params);
    }
```

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add a whitelist to validate `CallParams.target`.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/utilities/FeeWrapper.sol#L66


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Attacker can abuse the arbitrary call of `FeeWrapper.sol` contract to other contract to call transferFrom and steal other users funds/tokens

## Proof of Concept
The `FeeWrapper.sol` contract have the `rubicall` function for users to charge their own fees, this function takes a `CallParams` struct with target (address to call), selector (function to execute) and args (function's args) on behalf the `FeeWrapper` contract, 
the contract also have the `_chargeFee` function of the fee charging (free transfer), as it uses the well known allowance and transferFrom mechanism `IERC20(_feeToken).transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), _totalAmount);`, now with all of this the following scenario can occurs :

1. Alice wants to charge fee for TokenX with worth of 50 TokenX, she have 3050 TokenX
2. she calls `rubicall` which calls `_rubicall` that calls `_chargeFee`
3. `_chargeFee` will `transferFrom` Alice to `FeeWrapper.sol` on the TokenX, which ensure that Alice must have approved `FeeWrapper.sol` to spend on her behalf on TokenX (she set allowance to type(uint256).max)
4. her call succeed, now she is allowing `FeeWrapper.sol` to spend `type(uint256).max` on TokenX, and she already have 3000 worth of TokenX
5. Bob (attacker) now calls the rubicall with TokenX (repeat the steps from 2 to 4 for bob) and set the `CallParams` as :

```
 selector = 0x23b872dd // which calls the transferFrom
 args = abi.encodeWithSignature("address,address,uint256") with 1st address of Alice and 2nd to Bob and  uint256 as 3000  // which calls transferFrom(Alice,BoB,3000) on the TokenX
 target = TokenX contract // target contract to call the transferFrom
 feeParams = add any
```

6. Since Alice have approval to `FeeWrapper.sol` to spend on her behalf, Bob will make the arbitrary call to TokenX to abuse this approval, and will successfully hijack 3000 tokens from Alice 
 


## Tools Used
Manual review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
For the data calls create an isolated contract (such as multicall) which don't have any permission approval or funds to hold

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The impact of this vulnerability is that the second user attempting to execute a token swap might encounter a failed `safeApprove()` call. This failure can result in unintended behavior, disrupting the expected flow of token swapping and potentially leading to transaction reverts.


## Proof of Concept
In the smart contract `ZetaTokenConsumerPancakeV3`, there is a potential vulnerability arising from the repeated use of `safeApprove()` without resetting the allowance to zero. Specifically, this issue occurs in functions that involve token swaps (`getZetaFromToken`, `getEthFromZeta`, and `getTokenFromZeta`).

The vulnerability stems from the fact that when multiple users interact with the contract using the same tokens, the second user's `safeApprove()` call may fail if the token allowance is not reset to zero before attempting to set a new allowance. This is particularly crucial when dealing with the same tokens, as approvals are not reset between different users' transactions.
## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It is imperative to reset the token allowance to zero before making subsequent `safeApprove()` calls. This ensures that the approval is explicitly revoked before granting it again.

## Impact

1. If the protocol doesn't have any ETH, then user's tx will revert


## Proof of Concept
Take [BranchBridgeAgent.callOutSignedAndBridge](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L276-L303) as an example, while a user Alice calls the function with properly parameters on Branch chain, and she sends enough gas for `BranchBridgeAgent.callOutSignedAndBridge`, the tx is executed successfully, and the messages will cross chain to Root branch.
In Root chain, [RootBridgeAgent.sol#L577-L617](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/RootBridgeAgent.sol#L577-L617) will handle Alice's message,

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

When a user wants to send funds from Root to Branch they call `RootBridgeAgent.callOutAndBridge()`. In the case of where this transferral of funds fails, the user can call `RootBridgeAgent.retrySettlement()`. However, an attacker can abuse the VirtualAccount from the victim by calling `VirtualAccount.payableCall()` in order to subsequently call `RootBridgeAgent.retrySettlement()` to claim the funds for themselves by specifying the `_recipient` to be themself. Thus the attacker steals funds from the user.

Note that the VirtualAccount from the victim user is allowed to call `RootBridgeAgent.retrySettlement()` because of line 248-250 in RootBridgeAgent:

```solidity
// RootBridgeAgent.sol
248            if (msg.sender != address(IPort(localPortAddress).getUserAccount(settlementReference.owner))) {
249                revert NotSettlementOwner();
250            }
```

## Proof of Concept

The POC below is doing the following: 

* Funds are first bridged from the AVAX branch to root.

* Then subsequently bridged back from root to AVAX branch by MulticallRootRouter using `RootBridgeAgent.callOutAndBridge()`, which is failing.

* Then the attacker calls `VirtualAccount.payableCall()` which calls `RootBridgeAgent.retrySettlement()` and specifying themself as recipient.

* As a result the attacker gets minted the victim users funds on the branch.

Consider adding the `requiresApprovedCaller` access control modifier to `VirtualAccount.payableCall()` so that the attacker can't abuse this function.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L770
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/RootBridgeAgent.sol#L823


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Due to lack of an estimation of the exact gas fee on the destination chain, the transaction of the LayerZeroEndpoint#`send()` called via the BranchBridgeAgent#`_performCall()` would be reverted.


## Proof of Concept

Within the BranchBridgeAgent#`_performCall()`, the LayerZeroEndpoint#`send()` would be called like this:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L770
```solidity
    /**
     * @notice Internal function performs the call to LayerZero messaging layer Endpoint for cross-chain messaging.
     *   @param _refundee address to refund excess gas to.
     *   @param _payload params for root bridge agent execution.
     *   @param _gParams LayerZero gas information. (_gasLimit,_remoteBranchExecutionGas,_nativeTokenRecipientOnDstChain)
     */
    function _performCall(address payable _refundee, bytes memory _payload, GasParams calldata _gParams)
        internal
        virtual
    {
        //Sends message to LayerZero messaging layer
        ILayerZeroEndpoint(lzEndpointAddress).send{value: msg.value}( ///<---------- @audit
            rootChainId,
            rootBridgeAgentPath,
            _payload,
            payable(_refundee),
            address(0),
            abi.encodePacked(uint16(2), _gParams.gasLimit, _gParams.remoteBranchExecutionGas, rootBridgeAgentAddress)
        );
    }
```

According to the ["Send Messages"](https://layerzero.gitbook.io/docs/evm-guides/master/how-to-send-a-message#estimating-message-fees) in the LayerZero's documentation, there is a way to calculate dynamic fee (icl. gas fee) to be paid on the destination chain like this:
> **Estimating Message Fees**
> If you want to know how much `{value: xxx}` to give to the `send()` function to pay for you message please refer to this [section on estimating fees](https://github.com/docs/evm-guides/code-examples/estimating-message-fees).

And then, according to the ["Estimating Message Fees"](https://layerzero.gitbook.io/docs/evm-guides/code-examples/estimating-message-fees) in the LayerZero's documentation, the `estimateFees()` function would be recommended to calculate a dynamic fee based on Oracle and Relayer prices for the destination chainId like this:
> The `estimateFees()` function returns a **dynamic fee** based on Oracle and Relayer prices for the **destination chainId**, your UserApplication contract, and payload parameters.

In addition to that, according to the ["Failure Revert Messages"](https://layerzero.gitbook.io/docs/evm-guides/error-messages/failure-revert-messages#layerzero-not-enough-native-for-fees) in the LayerZero's documentation, the `estimateFees()` function would be recommended to use in order to avoid the situation that there is not enough native tokens for fee on the destination chain like this:
> **LayerZero: not enough native for fees**
> User Application needs to send more `msg.value` (see: `Endpoint.estimateFees()`)

Based on the reference from the LayerZero's documentation above, the exact gas fee is supposed to be estimated when the LayerZeroEndpoint#`send()` would be called.

However, when the LayerZeroEndpoint#`send()` would be called in the BranchBridgeAgent#`_performCall()`, an arbitrary gas fee (`msg.value`) would just be assigned and sent to the destination chain.
This means that the exact `gas fee` on the destination chain would not be `estimated` when the LayerZeroEndpoint#`send()` would be called in the BranchBridgeAgent#`_performCall()`. 

This lead to reverting the transaction of the LayerZeroEndpoint#`send()` called via the BranchBridgeAgent#`_performCall()` due to an insufficient gas fee on the destination chain. 

Remarks:
- RootBridgeAgent#`_performCall()` has the same vulnerability.
  https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/RootBridgeAgent.sol#L823


## Tools Used
- Foundry


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Within the BranchBridgeAgent#`_performCall()`, consider calculating the exact `fee` on the destination chain via the LayerZeroEndpoint#`estimateFees()`.
And then, consider assign the calculated-fee of the native token into LayerZeroEndpoint#`send()` as an argument like this:
```diff
    function _performCall(address payable _refundee, bytes memory _payload, GasParams calldata _gParams)
        internal
        virtual
    {
+       uint256 fee = getFeeEstimate(_gParams.gasLimit, _gParams.remoteBranchExecutionGas, _payload)
    
        //Sends message to LayerZero messaging layer
+       ILayerZeroEndpoint(lzEndpointAddress).send{value: fee}(
-       ILayerZeroEndpoint(lzEndpointAddress).send{value: msg.value}(
            rootChainId,
            rootBridgeAgentPath,
            _payload,
            payable(_refundee),
            address(0),
            abi.encodePacked(uint16(2), _gParams.gasLimit, _gParams.remoteBranchExecutionGas, rootBridgeAgentAddress)
        );
    }
```

Remarks:
- RootBridgeAgent#`_performCall()` has same vulnerability. Thus, consider adding the same solution to there as well.

# Vulnerability details

Unlike the rest of the non-pure external functions in `VirtualAccount.sol`, `payableCall` is not making use of the `requiresApprovedCaller` modifier, thus not imposing any restrictions on `msg.sender`.

## Impact

The impact of this issue is huge, since it is trivial for anyone to execute arbitrary calls on behalf of the actual owner of the virtual account.

In particular, and since the VirtualAccount is expected to hold [ERC20](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/VirtualAccount.sol#L56), [ERC721](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/VirtualAccount.sol#L61) and [ERC1155](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/VirtualAccount.sol#L124-L141) tokens, an attacker can drain the balance of any of these tokens by making calls to their respective contracts through the `payableCall` function.

## Proof of Concept

description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/746905cdd3aa165ba1f9274c360dfd9f0c52e781/src/RootPort.sol#L165-L168

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

(Please Note: this finding is NOT related to the issue from the "Publicly Known Issues")

SUMMARY/DESCRIPTION:
The standard approach of solady's `renounceOwnership()` function is to remove the ability to change ownership after contract deployment/initialization, for security purposes and probably to help boost permissionless nature of protocols.

However, since it seems the Ulysses protocol has decided not to implement this functionality for these affected contracts (yet), the devs made it impossible to renounce ownership by adding the revert() statement to the two `renounceOwnership()` functions.

The idea was correct, but the implementation was incorrect.

RISKS/EFFECTS:

- It will be impossible to initialize many state variables from at least 6 contracts, effectively permanently DoS-ing many of the protocol's critical functionalities, including:

  -- `BaseBranchRouter` - For interfacing with Branch Bridge Agents.
  -- `BranchBridgeAgentFactory` - For allowing permissionless deployment of new Branch Bridge Agents.
  -- `ArbitrumBranchBridgeAgentFactory` - For allowing permissionless deployment of new Arbitrum Branch Bridge Agents.
  -- `MulticallRootRouter` - For interfacing with third-party dApps present in the Root Omnichain Environment.
  -- `ERC20hTokenBranchFactory` - For permissionless deployment of new Branch hTokens in Branch Chains of Ulysses Omnichain 
  -- `ERC20hTokenRootFactory` - For permissionless deployment of new Root hTokens in the Root Chain of Ulysses Omnichain

## Proof of Concept

The problem is that most of the initializable contracts' `initialize()` functions are calling this modified `renounceOwnership()` function, which will cause all these affected `initialize()` functions to permanently revert.

The following is the Ulysses protocol's modified implementation of the `renounceOwnership()` function from "solady/auth/Ownable.sol" library:
```solidity
    /// @notice Function being overriden to prevent mistakenly renouncing ownership.
    function renounceOwnership() public payable override onlyOwner {
        revert("Cannot renounce ownership"); 	/// @audit-issue this revert statement is problematic.
    }
```

The modified implementation above overrides the standard implementation below from "solady/auth/Ownable.sol" library:
```solidity
    /// @dev Allows the owner to renounce their ownership.
    function renounceOwnership() public payable virtual onlyOwner {
        _setOwner(address(0));
    }
```

One example of many: 

ERC20hTokenRootFactory::initialize()
```solidity
    /**
     * @notice Function to initialize the contract.
     * @param _coreRouter Address of the Root Chain's Core Router.
     */
    function initialize(address _coreRouter) external onlyOwner {
        require(_coreRouter != address(0), "CoreRouter address cannot be 0");
        coreRootRouterAddress = _coreRouter;
        renounceOwnership();    					/// @audit-issue this line will always revert
    }
```

All 6 affected initialize() functions/contracts:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/746905cdd3aa165ba1f9274c360dfd9f0c52e781/src/BaseBranchRouter.sol#L66
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/746905cdd3aa165ba1f9274c360dfd9f0c52e781/src/MulticallRootRouter.sol#L114
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/746905cdd3aa165ba1f9274c360dfd9f0c52e781/src/factories/ArbitrumBranchBridgeAgentFactory.sol#L67
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/746905cdd3aa165ba1f9274c360dfd9f0c52e781/src/factories/BranchBridgeAgentFactory.sol#L103
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/746905cdd3aa165ba1f9274c360dfd9f0c52e781/src/factories/ERC20hTokenBranchFactory.sol#L76
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/746905cdd3aa165ba1f9274c360dfd9f0c52e781/src/factories/ERC20hTokenRootFactory.sol#L52

## Tools Used
VSC. Manual.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Some options:
- either remove the `renounceOwnership()` method from the affected `initialize()` functions
or
- remove the revert() statement from the `renounceOwnership()` method, which I show below:

```solidity
    /// @notice Function being overriden to prevent mistakenly renouncing ownership.
    function renounceOwnership() public payable override onlyOwner {
    --  revert("Cannot renounce ownership");
    ++  // leave empty
    }
```
OR
```solidity
    /// @notice Function being overriden to prevent mistakenly renouncing ownership.
    function renounceOwnership() public payable override onlyOwner {
    --  revert("Cannot renounce ownership");
    ++  emit CannotRenounceOwnership(); /// @audit obviously this will require adding a new event
    }
```

This effectively eliminates the problem of most initialize() functions permanently reverting, and at the same time still prevents renouncing of ownership of these contracts. 
So the idea/intention of the devs is maintained, but without the revert bug, so the contracts/state variables can now be initialized without DoS-ing critical protocol functionalities.

# Lines of code

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The first byte of the message `_payload[0]` represents the type of message. If an exception occurs inside the message processing and the user wants to trigger Fallback, then the message type needs to be ORed with 0x80. For example, `0x05` represents the message type SignedWithDeposit and FallbackToggled is `false`. `(0x80 | 0x05) = 0x85` represents the message type SignedWithDeposit, and FallbackToggled is `true`.

However, in `RootBridgeAgent._createSettlementMultiple`, there is [an error](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/RootBridgeAgent.sol#L1090) in preparing data for call with settlement of multiple assets. The encoded message type is always 0x02 regardless of whether `_hasFallbackToggled` is true. This has the following impacts:

1.  `_hasFallbackToggled` is true. After the encoded message reaches the target BranchBridgeAgent, if an exception occurs inside the message processing, the fallback will not be triggered as expected.
2.  Since triggering fallback is equivalent to sending a cross-chain message, it requires a certain amount of gas. The protocol uses [Airdrop](https://layerzero.gitbook.io/docs/evm-guides/advanced/relayer-adapter-parameters#airdrop) to send messages. The relayer from Layerzero will send gas to the target BranchBridgeAgent before the message is processed. Failure to trigger fallback means that the gas will be left in the target BranchBridgeAgent.

## Proof of Concept

When a user can send multiple tokens from the ftm branch to the mainnet branch via [BranchBridgeAgent.callOutSignedAndBridgeMultiple](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L306-L312), the `_hasFallbackToggled` argument is `true`. And the user provides all the gas required for the entire process. This process requires two cross-chain messages: the first message is ftm branch -> arb root, and the second message is arb root -> mainnet branch.

**When the first message reaches RootBridgeAgent**, the processing flow is as follows:

```flow
RootBridgeAgent.lzReceive
  (bool success,) = address(this).excessivelySafeCall
    lzReceiveNonBlocking
      //_payload[0]=0x86 means _hasFallbackToggled = true
      _execute
        bridgeAgentExecutorAddress.call
          RootBridgeAgentExecutor.executeSignedWithDepositMultiple
            _bridgeInMultiple
            //has additional calldata because sending htoken to mainnet
            IRouter(_router).executeSignedDepositMultiple	//MulticallRootRouter
              // FUNC ID: 3 (multicallMultipleOutput)
              _approveMultipleAndCallOut
->              IBridgeAgent(_bridgeAgentAddress).callOutAndBridgeMultiple  //_bridgeAgentAddress=RootBridgeAgent
=>                _createSettlementMultiple
                  _performCall	//send message to dest branch
```

From the above process, we can see that `_createSettlementMultiple` is called in `RootBridgeAgent.callOutAndBridgeMultiple`, and the value of `_hasFallbackToggled` is passed in by `MulticallRootRouter._approveMultipleAndCallOut`. Let's take a look at its code:

```solidity
File: src\MulticallRootRouter.sol
544:     function _approveMultipleAndCallOut(
545:         address refundee,
546:         address recipient,
547:         address[] memory outputTokens,
548:         uint256[] memory amountsOut,
549:         uint256[] memory depositsOut,
550:         uint16 dstChainId,
551:         GasParams memory gasParams
552:     ) internal virtual {
......
565:         //Move output hTokens from Root to Branch and call 'clearTokens'.
566:         IBridgeAgent(_bridgeAgentAddress).callOutAndBridgeMultiple{value: msg.value}(
567:             payable(refundee),
568:             recipient,
569:             dstChainId,
570:             "",
571:             SettlementMultipleInput(outputTokens, amountsOut, depositsOut),
572:             gasParams,
573:->           true	//this param is _hasFallbackToggled
574:         );
575:     }
```

L573, `_hasFallbackToggled` is always set to `true`, indicating that if an exception occurs when the target branch handles the message, a fallback is expected to be triggered. However, the problem lies in the incorrect encoding of the message type inside `_createSettlementMultiple`, which makes the fallback impossible to be triggered.

```solidity
File: src\RootBridgeAgent.sol
1045:     function _createSettlementMultiple(
......
1054:         bool _hasFallbackToggled
1055:     ) internal returns (bytes memory _payload) {
......
1087: 
1088:         // Prepare data for call with settlement of multiple assets
1089:         _payload = abi.encodePacked(
1090:->           _hasFallbackToggled ? bytes1(0x02) & 0x0F : bytes1(0x02),
1091:             _recipient,
1092:             uint8(hTokens.length),
1093:             _settlementNonce,
1094:             hTokens,
1095:             tokens,
1096:             _amounts,
1097:             _deposits,
1098:             _params
1099:         );
......
1114:     }
```

L1090, _hasFallbackToggled = true, so _payload[0] should be 0x82 instead of `bytes1(0x02) & 0xF = 0x02`.

**When the second message reaches mainnet BranchBridgeAgent**, the processing flow is as follows:

```flow
BranchBridgeAgent.lzReceive
  address(this).excessivelySafeCall  //using low-level call, so if there is revert inside, just return false.
    lzReceiveNonBlocking
      // DEPOSIT FLAG: 2 (Multiple Settlement)
      _execute  //_payload[0] == 0x02, so the _hasFallbackToggled argument in _execute is false
        (bool success,) = bridgeAgentExecutorAddress.call  //BranchBridgeAgentExecutor.executeWithSettlementMultiple
```

The message is finally processed in [BranchBridgeAgentExecutor.executeWithSettlementMultiple](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/BranchBridgeAgentExecutor.sol#L104). Let's look at the code of `_execute`:

```solidity
File: src\BranchBridgeAgent.sol
730:     function _execute(bool _hasFallbackToggled, uint32 _settlementNonce, address _refundee, bytes memory _calldata)
731:         private
732:     {
733:         //Update tx state as executed
734:         executionState[_settlementNonce] = STATUS_DONE;
735: 
736:         //Try to execute the remote request
737:         (bool success,) = bridgeAgentExecutorAddress.call{value: address(this).balance}(_calldata);
738: 
739:         //Update tx state if execution failed
740:->       if (!success) {
741:             //Read the fallback flag and perform the fallback call if necessary. If not, allow for retrying deposit.
742:->           if (_hasFallbackToggled) {
743:                 // Update tx state as retrieve only
744:                 executionState[_settlementNonce] = STATUS_RETRIEVE;
745: 
746:                 // Perform fallback call
747:                 _performFallbackCall(payable(_refundee), _settlementNonce);
748:             } else {
749:                 // If no fallback is requested revert allowing for settlement retry.
750:->               revert ExecutionFailure();
751:             }
752:         }
753:     }
```

L737, success will be `false` if processing this message has an error.

L742, `_hasFallbackToggled` is `false` because the message type is 0x02, so the fallback call will not be performed.

L750, `revert ExecutionFailure()` will make [address(this).excessivelySafeCall](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L579-L583) return `false`, so tx is executed successfully.

Through the above analysis, we can know that due to this wrong message encoding, the fallback is not triggered as expected. The gas required to trigger the fallback has been sent to BranchBridgeAgent, and these gases will remain in the contract, causing user gas losses.

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

```fix
File: src\RootBridgeAgent.sol
1089:         _payload = abi.encodePacked(
1090:-            _hasFallbackToggled ? bytes1(0x02) & 0x0F : bytes1(0x02),
1090:+            _hasFallbackToggled ? bytes1(0x82) : bytes1(0x02),
1091:             _recipient,
1092:             uint8(hTokens.length),
1093:             _settlementNonce,
1094:             hTokens,
1095:             tokens,
1096:             _amounts,
1097:             _deposits,
1098:             _params
1099:         );
```

Consider a situation where one of the calls made by multicall includes an interaction with a malicious contract. This malicious contract could be crafted to make a reentrant call back to the multicall function, potentially before the initial call has completed its execution. This reentrancy could lead to unexpected behavior, such as manipulating state variables or triggering functions in an unintended order.

Manual review

The multicall function in the contract allows for executing multiple calls in a single transaction. However, it lacks a check on the size of the input array data. ```


## Proof of Concept

Exploit Scenario: An attacker crafts a data array with a very large number of elements and calls the multicall function. Each element in the array triggers a delegatecall, consuming gas. The cumulative gas cost of processing the large array can reach the block gas limit, causing the transaction to fail.

Manual review

Limit Array Size: Introduce a check to limit the size of the data array. This limit should be based on the average expected usage and the gas cost associated with each call within the array.
Gas Usage Monitoring: Implement a mechanism to monitor the cumulative gas used in each iteration of the loop within multicall. If the gas usage exceeds a certain threshold, the function can revert to prevent DoS attacks.
Testing: Conduct thorough testing with various array sizes to determine the optimal limit and ensure that legitimate use cases are not adversely affected.

This means that all the contributions will be forever locked in the contract, as there is also no receive() fallback that can be used to directly send the amount spent to make `finalize` possible.


## Tools Used
Manual Review

Consider implementing any of these:
- ETHCrowdfundBase should have a receive() callback
- Instead of transferring totalContributions, finalize should transfer `address(this).balance` or `min(totalContributions,address(this).balance)`

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/main/contracts/party/PartyGovernance.sol#L451-L453
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/main/contracts/party/PartyGovernanceNFT.sol#L451-L455


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Party Proposals can be maliciously completed, allowing for the approval of unwanted proposals within the Party governance system.

## Explanation
In the Party, members can delegate their intrinsic voting power to a new address, removing it from the old one (if any) via [`delegateVotingPower()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/main/contracts/party/PartyGovernance.sol#L451-L453) function and transfer their governance NFTs (voting power) via [`transferFrom`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/main/contracts/party/PartyGovernanceNFT.sol#L451-L455) function.

```js
    /// @notice Pledge your intrinsic voting power to a new delegate, removing it from
    ///         the old one (if any).
    /// @param delegate The address to delegate voting power to.
    function delegateVotingPower(address delegate) external {
        _adjustVotingPower(msg.sender, 0, delegate);
    }
```

```js
    function transferFrom(address owner, address to, uint256 tokenId) public override {
        // Transfer voting power along with the token.
        _transferVotingPower(owner, to, votingPowerByTokenId[tokenId]);
        super.transferFrom(owner, to, tokenId);
    }
```

The issue arises when there is an active proposal, and Party members delegate or transfer their governance NFTs (voting power). Currently, the voting power is not immediately removed from the total votes of the active proposal, potentially leading to the malicious completion of a proposal that may not align with the Party's consensus.

## Proof of Concept
Let's consider the following example:

| Member               | Voting Power |
|----------------------|--------------|
| Alice (party member) | 100          |
| Bob (party member)   | 200          |
| Kevin (party member) | 50           |
| Steve (party member) | 50           |
| totalVotingPower     | 400          |
| passThresholdBps     | 1000         |

1. Alice creates a proposal. At this point, Alice's proposal has `100 votes`.
2. Kevin and Steve do not support Alice's proposal and do not approve it.
3. Bob supports Alice's proposal and `accepts` it. Now, Alice's proposal has `300 votes`.
4. However, Bob wants this proposal to be completed at any cost. He creates a second account named Danny, delegates his `200 voting power` to Danny (his second address), and calls the `accept()` function again. As a result, Alice's proposal now has `500 votes` and can be completed.

The core issue lies in the fact that when voting power is `delegated` or `transferred` within the Party between addresses, the `voting power` of these users is not immediately deducted from the total votes of the current active proposal.

## Tool Used
Manual Inspection

## Recommendation and Migration Steps
Immediate Vote Adjustment: Ensure that when a Party member delegates or transfers their voting power, it is immediately adjusted and deducted from the total votes of any active proposals. This should be done synchronously as part of the delegation or transfer process to prevent manipulation of active proposals.

With current impplmentation in contracts where openzeppelin ownable.sol is used, the owner is defaulted to address(0) due to not being set in constructor during deployement.

Considering for example:
In AmphoraProtocolToken.sol, With current impplmentation the owner is defaulted to address(0) due to not being set in constructor during deployement.

```Solidity

8 contract AmphoraProtocolToken is IAmphoraProtocolToken, ERC20VotesComp, Ownable {
9   constructor(
10    address _account,
11    uint256 _initialSupply
12  ) ERC20('Amphora Protocol', 'AMPH') ERC20Permit('Amphora Protocol') {

15
```

```Solidity
constructor(address initialOwner) {

}
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-amphora/blob/daae020331404647c661ab534d20093c875483e1/core/solidity/contracts/core/WUSDA.sol#L247


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`VaultController::_getPriceWithDecimals` is intended to return the decimal-adjusted price of a token; however, the decimal adjustment is incorrect and results in an inflated price for non-18 decimal tokens. Here, `_price` is the raw oracle price of the token normalized to 18 decimals:

```solidity
function _getPriceWithDecimals(uint256 _price, uint256 _decimals) internal pure returns (uint256 _priceWithDecimals) {
    _priceWithDecimals = _price * 10 ** (18 - _decimals); // @audit - this should be divide. e.g. 18 dec price -> 6 dec token = 1e18 / 1e18 - 1e6 = 1e18 / 1e12 = 1e6, but this is 1e18 * 1e12 = 1e30
  }
```

This function returns the correct value for 18 decimal tokens, as the additional factor simply becomes 1, but should instead return `_price / 10 ** (18 - decimals)` for non-18 decimal tokens rather than multiplying by this factor. For example, USDC is a 6 decimal token, so the price should be divided by `10^12` to get the correct price. Instead, the price is multiplied by `10^12`, resulting in a price that is `10^24` times too high (1e18 * 1e12 / 1e6). This results in an inflated borrowing power for non-18 decimal tokens and a lower `maxTokensToLiquidate` in liquidation math.

**_borrowing:_**
1e6 USDC is now worth 1e42 USDA rather than 1e18 USDA. Assume the vault has a balance of 1M USDC, or 1e12 USDC, its borrowing power is calculated to be 1e48 USDA rather than 1e24 USDA. This means the vault can borrow 1e48 USDA, which is 1e24 times more than it should be able to borrow.

This issue is even further exacerbated by lower decimal tokens such as GUSD. Additionally, if the minter chose to borrow only a fraction of the available USDA, they could effectively open a position that is highly unlikely to ever be liquidated.

**_liquidating:_**
So long as the minter borrows more USDA than the true value of that in their vault, the real collateral value is never enough to cover the debt to begin with, but the vault will not be liquidatable until the reported price of the collateral drops by a significant factor, and only then will a factor of `10^24` the value be recoverable. This is because the vault's borrowing power is inflated by 1e24 times, so in the example above the vault can borrow 10^30 USDA tokens, but only has 1M USDC to cover the debt.

Furthermore, this faulty price adjustment is used in the calculations of `VaultController::_calculateTokensToLiquidate` which is used to determine the maximum amount of collateral that can be liquidated from a vault, meaning that the vault can only be liquidated for a fraction of the collateral that it should be liquidated for based on the true LTV in the event a significant price change pushes the vault's borrowing power below its USDA liability.

```solidity
function _amountToSolvency(uint96 _id) internal returns (uint256 _usdaToSolvency) {
    _usdaToSolvency = _vaultLiability(_id) - _getVaultBorrowingPower(_getVault(_id)); // @audit - will underflow and revert if borrowing power exceeds liability, even if true LTV is above liquidation threshold
}
```

If this is not the case, either because the vault has not borrowed the maximum amount of USDA or because the price change is not significant enough, the vault will never be liquidated due to underflow in the liquidation math causing a revert. For tokens such as USDC which are intended to be stable around $1, this is unlikely to occur, and even in a depeg event the inflated borrowing power would likely be enough to cover the USDA liability, potentially even allowing a malicious user to deposit depegged-USDC and borrow more USDA to be redeemed for sUSD at the actual dollar peg.

## Proof of Concept
* Vault holds 1M USDC.
* Vault can borrow 10^30 USDA tokens.
* Vault should only be able to borrow 1M (1e24) USDA tokens.
* Vault borrows max amount of USDA available.
* Minter redeems USDA for sUSD and makes a massive profit.

## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```diff
- _priceWithDecimals = _price * 10 ** (18 - _decimals);
+ _priceWithDecimals = _price / 10 ** (18 - _decimals);
```

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details

The `registerErc20` and `updateRegisteredErc20` functions do not include a check to ensure that the `_oracleAddress` provided is the intended Oracle for the token being registered or updated.

## Impact

Setting an incorrect Oracle for a token, whether newly registered or updated, can lead to token overvaluation/undervaluation. 

This situation could allow any user to increase their borrowing power or liquidate other users with undervalued vaults. 

The resulting fallout could lead to significant losses for the protocol or individual users.

## Proof of Concept

Consider the following scenario:

1. An owner executes an `updateRegisteredErc20()` operation to refresh `WETH` information with updated collateral data. Unfortunately, the `_oracleAddress` used pertains to the `WBTC` oracle.
2. A malicious user leverages a flash loan of `WETH`. They establish a new vault, deposit `WETH` into it exploiting the incorrect pricing, and take out a loan in `sUSD`, thereby draining all USDA reserves. The malicious user then repays the flash loan, harvesting the profits.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Ensure that `IOracleRelay(_oracleAddress).underlying()` matches `_tokenAddresses` within the `registerErc20` and `updateRegisteredErc20` functions.

```diff
function registerErc20(
    address _tokenAddress,
    uint256 _ltv,
    address _oracleAddress,
    uint256 _liquidationIncentive,
    uint256 _cap,
    uint256 _poolId
) external override onlyOwner {
+   if (IOracleRelay(_oracleAddress).underlying() != _tokenAddress) revert VaultController_IncorrectOracle();
```

```diff
function updateRegisteredErc20(
    address _tokenAddress,
    uint256 _ltv,
    address _oracleAddress,
    uint256 _liquidationIncentive,
    uint256 _cap,
    uint256 _poolId
) external override onlyOwner {
+   if (IOracleRelay(_oracleAddress).underlying() != _tokenAddress) revert VaultController_IncorrectOracle();
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Although unlikely, depeg events of stablecoins can occur, and have actually already occurred several times in the past. Currently the `USDA` contract has no protection against that, other than the pause/unpause functionality, which is also not perfect, since it locks both the deposit and **withdrawal** functionality.
This means that if a depeg were to happen, either the `USDA` contract will be paused (assuming that the protocol team monitors the market carefully and reacts in a timely manner), making users unable to withdraw their funds, or users will be able to mint new USDA tokens at a discount, if the contract does not get paused.

## Proof of Concept

With the current implementation of the `USDA` contract, there are two detrimental scenarios that can play out in the event of a sUSD depeg:

1. The protocol team reacts quickly and pauses the contract when sUSD reaches a price of, let's say, 0.95 USD. However, there is a chance that the token might never recover from the depeg and keep on going down, until it reaches a price that is close to 0. Such was the case with the USTC token when the Luna crash happened. This means that, in such scenario, users will end up loosing all of the assets that they deposited, since they didn't have a chance to react and withdraw their assets, due to the pause.
2. The protocol team does not react on time and the contract stays unpaused. In this scenario, users will be able to deposit sUSD tokens, that are currently worth less and in turn, mint USDA tokens at a discount.

## Tools used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To mitigate this issue, at the beginning of all deposit functions, you should fetch the sUSD price from a trusted oracle source, check it against a predefined min price, and revert if it is bellow that.
Additionally, you may also want to create separate pausing mechanisms for the withdraw and deposit functionalities.
