# Vulnerability details

## Impact
- The external Chainlink oracle, which provides index price information to the system, introduces risk inherent to any dependency on third-party data sources. For example, the oracle could fall behind or otherwise fail to be maintained, resulting in outdated data being fed to protocol.
- Stale prices could put funds at risk. According to Chainlink's documentation, This function does not error if no answer has been reached but returns 0, causing an incorrect price fed to the PriceOracle. The external Chainlink oracle, which provides index price information to the system, introduces risk inherent to any dependency on third-party data sources. For example, the oracle could fall behind or otherwise fail to be maintained, resulting in outdated data being fed to protocol
- Chainlink aggregators have a built in circuit breaker if the price of an asset goes outside of a predetermined price band. The result is that if an asset experiences a huge drop in value (i.e. LUNA crash) the price of the oracle will continue to return the minPrice instead of the actual price of the asset. This would allow user to continue borrowing with the asset but at the wrong price. This is exactly what happened to [Venus on BSC when LUNA imploded](https://rekt.news/venus-blizz-rekt/).

## Proof of Concept
I) Lack of check return data from chainlink aggregators in `ChainlinkStalePriceLib.sol#getCurrentPrice()` allows a stale price to be used.
```
File: ChainlinkStalePriceLib.sol
11:  function getCurrentPrice(AggregatorV2V3Interface _aggregator) internal view returns (uint256 _price) {
12:    (, int256 _answer,,,) = _aggregator.latestRoundData();
13:    if (_answer <= 0) revert Chainlink_NegativePrice();
14:    _price = uint256(_answer);
15:  }
```
In the current implementation of [ChainlinkStalePriceLib.sol#getCurrentPrice()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-amphora/blob/179384321c36b669f48bc0485bbc1f807fba8fac/core/solidity/contracts/periphery/oracles/ChainlinkStalePriceLib.sol#L11-L15), there is no freshness check. This could lead to stale prices being used.
If the market price of the token drops very quickly ("flash crashes"), and Chainlink's feed does not get updated in time, the smart contract will continue to believe the token is worth more than the market value.
Chainlink also advise developers to check for the `updatedAt` before using the price:
```
Your application should track the latestTimestamp variable or use the updatedAt value from the latestRoundData() function to make sure that the latest answer is recent enough for your application to use it. If your application detects that the reported answer is not updated within the heartbeat or within time limits that you determine are acceptable for your application, pause operation or switch to an alternate operation mode while identifying the cause of the delay.
```
And they have this heartbeat concept:
```
Chainlink Price Feeds do not provide streaming data. Rather, the aggregator updates its latestAnswer when the value deviates beyond a specified threshold or when the heartbeat idle time has passed. You can find the heartbeat and deviation values for each data feed at data.chain.link or in the Contract Addresses lists.
```
II) `ChainlinkStalePriceLib.sol#getCurrentPrice()` will use the wrong price if the `aggregator` returns price outside `min/max` range.
```
File: ChainlinkStalePriceLib.sol
11:  function getCurrentPrice(AggregatorV2V3Interface _aggregator) internal view returns (uint256 _price) {
12:    (, int256 _answer,,,) = _aggregator.latestRoundData();
13:    if (_answer <= 0) revert Chainlink_NegativePrice();
14:    _price = uint256(_answer);
15:  }
```
- In the current implementation of [ChainlinkStalePriceLib.sol#getCurrentPrice()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-amphora/blob/179384321c36b669f48bc0485bbc1f807fba8fac/core/solidity/contracts/periphery/oracles/ChainlinkStalePriceLib.sol#L11-L15), there is only a check for `_answer` to be non-negative, and not within an acceptable range.
- `ChainlinkAggregators` have `minPrice` and `maxPrice` circuit breakers built into them. This means that if the price of the asset drops below the `minPrice`, the protocol will continue to value the token at `minPrice` instead of it's actual value. This will allow users to take out huge amounts of bad debt and bankrupt the protocol.

## Tools Used
Manual review and [Chainlink's docs](https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/api-reference)
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
- Add additional validation to check if the price is stale and round is complete.
- Should check the returned answer against the `minPrice/maxPrice` and revert if the answer is outside of the bounds.
Ex: Add constant `PRICE_ORACLE_STALE_THRESHOLD` and check:
```
+    (, int256 _answer, , uint256 updatedAt, ) = _aggregator.latestRoundData();
    
+   if (_answer >= maxPrice || _answer <= minPrice) revert();
+   if (block.timestamp - updatedAt > PRICE_ORACLE_STALE_THRESHOLD) revert();
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In zkSync it's not possible to find out that if a L2 transaction has been included in the block/batch and what was the transaction execution result from the L1 published and verified information!! this breaks one of the blockchain fundamental concepts: availability. the blockchain data should be available for everyone in L1 so the security and availability of the zkSync match the security and availability of Ethereum.

zkSync is L2 layer over Ethereum. it is supposed to be compatible with Ethereum, users would submit transaction and their transaction get included in blocks and users can verify that their transactions are mined and accepted by blockchain. being able to verify transaction inclusion and transaction result verify is one of the important fundamental feature of the Ethereum and all other the blockchains(except some privacy blockchains).

zkSync is not privacy blockchain and this behavior of zkSync is not like Ethereum. This would create a lot of problems for users. practically no off-chain user or program work with this blockchain. the only one know the transactions inside a batch is operator and others need to trust and rely on the operator. operator can deny or censors information from others.

to give more example:
- wallets and user will not know that if user transaction included in the block or not(because multiple transaction with same nonce can exists so nonce is not reliable and definite proof of inclusion)
- wallet and user will not know the result(revert or success) of their transaction (again nonce is not good at all, because reverted transaction would increase the nonce too)
- a user can't prove that he sent ETH to some one.
- a payment service can't distinguish received funds.
- block explorers won't work.

all this issues and because project wants users to save `$0.015` in each transactions. 

I believe this has High severity in current system and it has very bad impact on the users of the blockchain. a lot of bug and issue would happen because of this hidden-transaction. the team may say that they will fix it in the future and there will be some solutions, but that doesn't remove the issue right now.
they may also say it is a trade off between availability and low cost but the better deigns would be allow users to specify in transaction if they want to publish transaction hash or not(user would have paid 20B(truncated hash) more pubdata gas if he set the publish flag to true).

as another note: publishing L2 transactions will require sending 32 byte to Ethereum which will cost 32*17 gas and with price of 20GWei per gas we will have `32*17*20` Gwei cost and if ETH was $1600 then the whole price will be: $0.017, it means because of less than 2 cent, user won't see his transaction result and all the other impacts. (not to mention that publishing 20byte of transaction hash would be enough too and cost would be smaller too)

## Proof of Concept
According to the doc the pubdata only consist of `l2Tol1Logs <> l2Tol1Messages <> publishedBytecodes <> stateDiffs` and operator doesn't need to publish L2 transaction hashes that are included in the batch. so from public onchain data there isn't a way to find out which transactions are included in the batch.

the stateDiffs shows the nonce value of each address, but nonce value doesn't specify the whole transaction data that is executed. for example a user can have 5 transaction with the same nonce and if nonce increase it means 1 of them is executed.
so in current design there is no way to find out which L2 transaction are included in the block. also there is no way to find out about transaction result users would not know if their transaction has successfully executed or reverted.

balance changes can't show the transaction results too, for example if address A has a transaction that sends 20ETH to B and address B has a transaction sends 20ETH to C then if address B doesn't increase after the batch doesn't mean that A->B transaction was failed, maybe A->B and B->C both was successful. so the B balance itself doesn't show the real transaction result of the A->B (with C balance can find out the this two transaction results but this is just a simple example to show that destination balance doesn't show transaction success or failer)

each transaction hash is 32B and if we truncate, it will be 20B. submitting 20B for each Tx is not that much high and users can decide pay it or not. the max batch pubdata is 120K and adding 20K to it is only about 16% increase(assuming most of the time the pubdata will be full) so the cost of transaction only increase about 16% but availability will be like of Ethereum but in current design the availability is 0 and cost is 16% more efficient.

the other point is that publishing transaction hash can be optional and users decide based on a flag in their transaction. it's possible to send L2ToL1message right now but the problem with that is: first only contracts can do it, user can't publish L2ToL1 messages in simple ETH transfer. second problem is that it require at least 94 byte pubdata compare to 20 byte truncated transaction hash is a lot more.

VIM

give users option to publish their transaction hash in pubdata. (by adding a flag in the transaction struct)
add new segment to pubdata that shows the L2 transaction hashes.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-zksync/blob/1fb4649b612fac7b4ee613df6f6b7d921ddd6b0d/code/contracts/ethereum/contracts/zksync/facets/Admin.sol#L44-L50


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Granting and revoking a role for a user should be restricted to privileged or upper-level users, and it should not be granted to the same/same level of users.

The `setPendingAdmin()` function is designed to facilitate the change of the admin, a process that can be initiated by either the governor or the existing admin user. The nominated new admin can then accept the proposal by invoking the `acceptAdmin()` function.

This vulnerability arises from the fact that the existing admin can invoke the `setPendingAdmin()` function and modify `s.pendingAdmin` according to their preference, whether **intentionally or unintentionally**. This can occur even when the governor has already proposed a new admin. While the likelihood of this issue is deemed rare (as indicated in this [documentation](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-zksync/blob/main/docs/Smart%20contract%20Section/L1%20smart%20contracts.md#adminfacet)), it has the potential to allow the existing admin to front-run and, delay or overrule the governor's intended action of changing the admin to a new one. The existing admin can persistently set a new pending admin, thereby obstructing the actual new admin from accepting the role. This scenario may result in an indefinite delay of the governor's decision to change the admin, effectively allowing the existing admin to maintain their role indefinitely by overruling the execution of governors' `setPendingAdmin()`.

While the likelihood of this issue might be low and not causing any financial loss, it still a straightforward case of inappropriate access control in the contract, introducing the risk of undesired disruptions. Therefore, this issue is reported as having a medium severity.

## Proof of Concept

In `Admin.sol`, the governor act as the privileged user, has exclusive access to all the functions defined in this contract. As a privileged user, the governor's actions should remain inviolable, devoid of any overruling, delays, or restrictions under any circumstances. However, an inappropriate access control oversight in the `setPendingAdmin()` function can lead to the governor's desire to change the admin being either intentionally or unintentionally overridden, delayed, or restricted by the current admin user.

Refer to the following code snippet, which represents the implementation of the setPendingAdmin function:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-zksync/blob/1fb4649b612fac7b4ee613df6f6b7d921ddd6b0d/code/contracts/ethereum/contracts/zksync/facets/Admin.sol#L44C1-L50C6

```solidity

File: code/contracts/ethereum/contracts/zksync/facets/Admin.sol

44:    function setPendingAdmin(address _newPendingAdmin) external onlyGovernorOrAdmin {
45:        // Save previous value into the stack to put it into the event later
46:        address oldPendingAdmin = s.pendingAdmin;
47:        // Change pending admin
48:        s.pendingAdmin = _newPendingAdmin;
49:        emit NewPendingGovernor(oldPendingAdmin, _newPendingAdmin);

```

The access control assigned to the `setPendingAdmin` is `onlyGovernorOrAdmin`, allowing both the governor and admin to execute this function.

Here, two scenarios illustrate how the admin, whether accidentally or intentionally, can override the governor's wishes.

### Scenario 1:

1. The Governor proposes a new admin by calling `setPendingAdmin()`.
2. Unaware of the governor's transaction, the admin proposes another address as the new admin.

In this scenario, the admin's proposal unintentionally overrides the governor's proposal, despite the governor having higher privileges.

### Scenario 2:

1. The Governor identifies that the existing admin has become a malicious actor (e.g., __account/accounts compromised [very unlike situation in multisig]__ ) and initiates a proposal to change the current admin.
2. The malicious admin, detecting the governor's action, front-runs the governor's `setPendingAdmin()` transaction.
3. The malicious admin promptly calls `setPendingAdmin()` to set themselves as the `pendingAdmin`, thereby overwriting the governor's action.

In this case, the governor's proposal is intentionally overridden by the actions of the malicious admin.

Both the above scenarios are explaining how the admin is accidentally or intentionally overrule governors wish. 

**Note: While these scenarios are considered highly unlikely due to the utilization of the same multi-signature accounts/contracts, it's crucial to acknowledge that the contract still retains these vulnerabilities.**

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

1. The admin can revoke the admin role of the current admin by proposing himself as the new admin and accepting the proposal within a single transaction.
2. To mitigate the risk of misuse by overruling or delaying the governor's decision to set a new admin, access to the `setPendingAdmin()` function should be restricted solely to the governor using the `onlyGovernor` modifier.
3. Alternatively, consider implementing an approval mechanism that requires the governor's endorsement for an admin's proposal to set a new admin. This approach helps prevent situations where the governor's decision may be overruled.


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `AuctionHouse` contract implements a Dutch auction mechanism to recover debt from collateral. However, there is no check for sequencer uptime, which could lead to auctions failing or executing at unfavorable prices. 

The current deployment parameters allow auctions to succeed without a loss to the protocol for a duration of 10m 50s. If there's no bid on the auction after this period, the protocol has no other option but to take a loss or forgive the loan. This could have serious consequences in the event of a network outage, as any loss results in the slashing of all users with weight on the term. 

Network outages and large reorgs happen with relative frequency. For instance, Arbitrum suffered an hour-long outage just two weeks ago ([source](https://github.com/ArbitrumFoundation/docs/blob/50ee88b406e6e5f3866b32d147d05a6adb0ab50e/postmortems/15_Dec_2023.md)).

## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenario:

1. A loan is called and an auction is initiated.
2. The network experiences an outage, causing the sequencer to go offline.
3. The auction fails to receive any bids within the 10m 50s window due to the outage.
4. The protocol is forced to take a loss (if there's still a bid after the `midPoint` and before the auction ends) or forgive the loan, both leading to the complete slashing of all users with weight on the term.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To mitigate this issue, consider integrating an external uptime feed such as [Chainlink's L2 Sequencer Feeds](https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/l2-sequencer-feeds). This would allow the contract to invalidate an auction if the sequencer was ever offline during its duration. Alternatively, implement a mechanism to restart an auction if it has received no bids.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/main/src/loan/AuctionHouse.sol#L118-L161


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Since the anticipated deployment of Ethereum Credit Guild on the Ethereum mainnet and L2s like Arbitrum, we must consider the existence of the Sequencer and the risks it may pose. While using Dutch Auctions on L2s, we notice that the sequencer uptime isn't taken into account, but similar to what occurred on the [Arbitrum network on December 15th](https://dedaub.com/blog/arbitrum-sequencer-outage), the sequencer outage is a possibility for the future.

In a case where there are ongoing auctions while the sequencer is offline, the auction prices will continue to decrease during the sequencer is offline. When the sequencer comes back online, users will have the opportunity to bid these auctions at prices significantly lower than the market rate. This may actually even be the favorable outcome, as missing out entirely on the auction is also a possibility. Referring to the example mentioned in [AuctionHouse.sol#L33-L37](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/main/src/loan/AuctionHouse.sol#L33-L37), considering a 30-minute auction with a midPoint of 10 minutes and 50 seconds, if the sequencer remains inactive for just 11 minutes (passing the `midPoint`) it could lead to bad prices and if it stays offline for the entire 30 minutes, it would lead to forced debt forgiveness through `forgive()`. The size of bad debts can be anything and can have a dramatic impact considering the importance of their liquidation to the health of the protocol.

## Proof of Concept

Read the scenario above and [you can also take a look at this report where a similar case occurred.](https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2023-06-Index-judging/issues/40)

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Determine the maximum tolerable delay for the sequencer (11 minutes may be a good choice) and invalidate the auction if the sequencer was down for maximum tolerable delay or more during the auction period.

Here `collateralToBorrower` is a part of the total collateral amount auctioned given bidder only receives a portion of the collateral, but `creditAsked` is the full amount
- If bid occurs AFTER mid point, `collateralReceived` is always the full amount, but `creditAsked` from bidder scales down with time based on time elasped. Here `collateralToBorrower` is zero, because all of the collateral is given to the bidder. The whole liquidation mechanism is reliant on auctions being called when either the gauge is offboarded or if a partial repay delay has not been met by the borrower as seen [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/main/src/loan/LendingTerm.sol#L652-L656). ```solidity require( GuildToken(refs.guildToken).isDeprecatedGauge(address(this)) || partialRepayDelayPassed(loanId), "LendingTerm: cannot call" ); ``` However, the check uses the `||` operator, which means for any lending term that integrates a partial repayment mechanism, the borrower will be incentivized to delibrately delay partial repayment so that their auction can be called and then subsequently front-run first bid to dutch auction after midpoint to gain profits in terms of repaying lesser credit token for borrowed positions. to receive a discounted payment a This is made even worst given the max delay can only be set once and cannot be changed after as seen [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/main/src/loan/LendingTerm.sol#L172), so admin potentially increasing delay to a very high value in an attempt to resolve this issue is not an option. ## Tools Used Manual Analysis ## Recommendation This is involves changes in design of protocol, so recommendations should be taken with discretion: - Depending on markets, only allow loan call auctions when a certain collateral ratio is reached that threatens bad debt for protocol - Perhaps all lending terms should be offboarded before allowing loans to be called for auction, even for lending terms where partial repayments are necessary. # Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/2376d9af792584e3d15ec9c32578daa33bb56b43/src/loan/AuctionHouse.sol#L144-L152
 https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/2376d9af792584e3d15ec9c32578daa33bb56b43/test/proposals/gips/GIP_0.sol#L175-L179


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Whales (accounts with significant cryptocurrency holdings) can exploit the current auction mechanics to guarantee profits through block stuffing.

This is particularly feasible due to the short duration of auctions, allowing these entities to manipulate auction outcomes in their favor.

## Proof of Concept

The protocol uses a Dutch auction format with two phases:

- **First Phase**: Bidders must pay the full debt amount. The collateral percentage starts at 0% and increases with each new block until the auction's midpoint.
- **Second Phase**: The protocol offers the full collateral and decreases the owed debt by a percentage in each new block, reaching 0% at auction's end. This implies that a bidder could eventually receive the collateral for free.

Bidders are disincentivized to participate in the first phase, as it generally results in a net loss unless there are force majeure market conditions.

Whales can use a block stuffing attack to win large auctions and acquire collateral at significantly reduced prices.

Example scenario:

1. Alice has the following bad debt which is auctioned off:
	- Collateral: 2,000,000 USDC
	- Debt: 1,000 WETH (1 WETH = 2,000 USDC)
2. There are no bidders in the first phase of the auction since this would result in a loss for the bidder.
2. The auction reaches its midpoint. Collateral cost reduces by ~1.14% every block. This is because the second phase is 1150 sec. (as per the `GIP_0.sol` deployment script), i.e. 88 blocks on Mainnet. The decay rate is thus 100% / 88 ~ 1.14%
3. At the auction's midpoint, Bob executes block stuffing attack. To make sure his attack would succeed, he uses a gas price of 250 Gwei.
4. After 88 blocks, Bob binds in the final block and wins 2,000,000 USDC at 0 ETH cost.

The attack cost is: 
$$
88\ blocks \times 30M\ gas\ \times 250\ Gwei = 66,000,000,000\ Gwei = 660\ ETH ~= 1.5M\ USDC
$$

Thus, Bob has made a profit of 500,000 USDC.

This strategy, while requiring substantial funds, is a feasible and potentially lucrative attack vector.

The severity is set to Medium given its low likelihood but high impact.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To mitigate this vulnerability, it is recommended to extend the auction duration. Longer auctions would increase the cost and complexity of block stuffing attacks, reducing the likelihood of such exploits.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/2376d9af792584e3d15ec9c32578daa33bb56b43/src/loan/AuctionHouse.sol#L166-L196


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Attackers could bid arbitrary amounts to acquire underpriced collateral, forcing bad debt losses. `bid()` function doesn't validate bid value to external pricing or fair market value.

## Proof of Concept

The `bid()` function facilitates users acquiring collateral from liquidated loan positions in exchange for repaying associated debt.  

**The core vulnerability is lacks validation on the bid amount compared to collateral value**. By failing to check bids against pricing oracles or reasonable ratios, attackers can distort bids.

For example:

1. Loan liquidates with 1000 ETH as collateral, worth $1500
2. Attacker bids 1000 ETH for only $750 of debt 
3. Contract accepts highly distorted bid
4. 1000 ETH moves to attacker for fractional value
5. Remaining debt marked as bad debt loss

This allows cheap seizure of collateral by manipulating bid prices: [AuctionHouse.sol.bid](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/2376d9af792584e3d15ec9c32578daa33bb56b43/src/loan/AuctionHouse.sol#L166-L196)

```solidity
function bid(bytes32 loanId) external {

  // No checks that bid makes sense vs collateral value
  // Enables heavily discounted collateral purchases
}
```
**Manipulating Auction Bids**

1. Loan liquidation happens for collateral worth 1000 ETH
2. 1000 ETH is worth $1500 at time of auction  

Normally this would fetch a bid near market rates:

```
Bidder bids 1000 ETH for $1490 worth of debt
Bid meets auction collateral ratio limits
Auction completes at fair ratio 
```

But by sending any unchecked bid amount, an attacker could manipulate:

```
Attacker bids 1000 ETH for $750 worth of debt  
No validation occurs on terrible ratio
Auction completes, bad debt realized
```

By failing to validate bids against an external pricing oracle or reasonable collateral ratio, the contract permits highly distorted bids.

This allows attackers to acquire collateral for way below true value, offloading the balance as bad debt and forcing a loss event.

## Tools Used

Vs

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Adding protections around expected bid ratios compared to real-time pricing is key to preventing manipulation.

1. Compare bid to oracle collateral ratios
2. Revert if bid price distorted
3. Maintain fair auction process

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

**Debt Value Invariant**

The debt value in stablecoin terms could shift if:

* The `SimplePSM` peg is manipulated by governance delays or front-running
* Bad debt accounting fails to properly markup positions

This could be exploited by borrowers artificially reducing debt values.

**SimplePSM Peg Manipulation**

The functions at risk are:

[SimplePSM.getMintAmountOut()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/2376d9af792584e3d15ec9c32578daa33bb56b43/src/loan/SimplePSM.sol#L80-L84)
[SimplePSM.getRedeemAmountOut()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/2376d9af792584e3d15ec9c32578daa33bb56b43/src/loan/SimplePSM.sol#L87-L93) 
[SimplePSM.mint()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/2376d9af792584e3d15ec9c32578daa33bb56b43/src/loan/SimplePSM.sol#L103-L112)
[SimplePSM.redeem()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/2376d9af792584e3d15ec9c32578daa33bb56b43/src/loan/SimplePSM.sol#L134-L144)

These calculations rely on the protocol `ProfitManager`'s credit multiplier to maintain a stable debt value peg. 

However, a governance delay in adjusting multiplier parameters downward could enable artificial redemption values.

**Bad Debt Accounting Failure**

Similarly, delays or sandwich attacks on `ProfitManager`'s [notifyPnL](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/2376d9af792584e3d15ec9c32578daa33bb56b43/src/governance/ProfitManager.sol#L292-L405) could fail to properly account for losses, enabling debt value manipulation.

## Proof of Concept

The `SimplePSM` and bad debt accounting logic relies on a synchronized state across protocol contracts. By sandwiching critical updates like credit multiplier adjustments or loss notifications, attackers can artificially shift debt token values off the peg.

**Manipulating the SimplePSM Peg** [getRedeemAmountOut](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/2376d9af792584e3d15ec9c32578daa33bb56b43/src/loan/SimplePSM.sol#L87-L93)

```solidity
function getRedeemAmountOut(
    uint256 amountIn
) public view returns (uint256) {
    uint256 creditMultiplier = ProfitManager(profitManager)
        .creditMultiplier();
    return (amountIn * creditMultiplier) / 1e18 / decimalCorrection;
}
```
Normally, `creditMultiplier` markdowns debt tokens if losses occur. But if an attacker sandwiches `ProfitManager` during a downgrade, `getRedeemAmountOut` will use the stale 1X multiplier, enabling full redemptions.

**Delaying Bad Debt Recognition** [notifyPnL](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-ethereumcreditguild/blob/2376d9af792584e3d15ec9c32578daa33bb56b43/src/governance/ProfitManager.sol#L292-L405)

```solidity
function notifyPnL(
        address gauge,
        int256 amount
    ) external onlyCoreRole(CoreRoles.GAUGE_PNL_NOTIFIER) {
  if (amount < 0) {
  
    // Shortfall logic

  }

}
```
If an attacker frontruns default notifications in `notifyPnL`, losses won't account. Debt positions appear healthier than they are, enabling manipulation.

Deferring critical state updates breaks sync between contracts, allowing debt values to shift off peg or avoid loss recognition. This subverts the invariant.

Vs

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Having critical calculations like `SimplePSM.getRedeemAmountOut()` dynamically fetch the latest `ProfitManager` state rather than use cached values. This reduces manipulation wiggle room.

Similarly, notifications like `ProfitManager.notifyPnL()` could trigger downstream updates like credit multiplier adjustments atomically.

**Also, consing the Use Chainlink Keepers**

For important asynchronous events like loss notifications, Chainlink Keepers can help unbiasably automate them to resist sandwich attacks.

title: Timeout values in Chainlink is hardcoded
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-badger/blob/main/packages/contracts/contracts/PriceFeed.sol#L561


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

A fixed timeout threshold might cause an incorrect staleness check leading to the wrong price being computed.

## Proof of Concept

In PriceFeed.sol, the timeout threshold for eth-btc feed and steth-eth feed is set as a constant

```
    // Maximum time period allowed since Chainlink's latest round data timestamp, beyond which Chainlink is considered frozen.
    uint256 public constant TIMEOUT_ETH_BTC_FEED = 4800; // 1 hours & 20min: 60 * 80
    uint256 public constant TIMEOUT_STETH_ETH_FEED = 90000; // 25 hours: 60 * 60 * 25
```

If the last updated time is greater than the timeout timing, then the feed is considered frozen.

```
    function _chainlinkIsFrozen(ChainlinkResponse memory _response) internal view returns (bool) {
        return
            _responseTimeout(_response.timestampEthBtc, TIMEOUT_ETH_BTC_FEED) ||
            _responseTimeout(_response.timestampStEthEth, TIMEOUT_STETH_ETH_FEED);
    }

    function _responseTimeout(uint256 _timestamp, uint256 _timeout) internal view returns (bool) {
        return block.timestamp - _timestamp > _timeout;
    }
```

The TIMEOUT variables are hardcoded and is a constant value, which will be an issue because Chainlink's heartbeat value might be changed in the future. For example, Chainlink may decrease the heartbeat for steth-eth oracle to 1 hour instead of the current 24 hours. If that's the case, then a check of 24 hours is extremely stale.

https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds

Changes are possible. Chainlink has changed their deviation threshold for Steth-eth from 2% to 0.5% before. 

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Allow the owner to update TIMEOUT_ETH_BTC_FEED and TIMEOUT_STETH_ETH_FEED in the contract.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-badger/blob/f2f2e2cf9965a1020661d179af46cb49e993cb7e/packages/contracts/contracts/PriceFeed.sol#L32-L33


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`TIMEOUT_ETH_BTC_FEED` and `TIMEOUT_STETH_ETH_FEED` are used as heartbeats to check if Chainlink prices are stale or not, but the periods used are bigger than it should which could lead to stale and wrong pricing.

## Proof of Concept
`PriceFeed.sol` is using ETH/BTC and STETH/ETH oracles from Chainlink to get the actual prices of those assets, prices which are used multiple times throughout the codebase. The problem relies in the fact the the values used to check if the prices are stale and Chainlink is frozen or not are not the right ones, which chainlink uses and recommends developers to use. As you can see, the values used are :
- 1 hour and 20 minutes for ETH/BTC oracle 
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-badger/blob/f2f2e2cf9965a1020661d179af46cb49e993cb7e/packages/contracts/contracts/PriceFeed.sol#L32
which is more than it should, as you can see on the Chainlink website, the heartbeat used for this oracle is only 1 hour https://data.chain.link/ethereum/mainnet/crypto-other/eth-btc
- 25 hours for STETH/ETH oracle
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-badger/blob/f2f2e2cf9965a1020661d179af46cb49e993cb7e/packages/contracts/contracts/PriceFeed.sol#L33
which is again more than it should, the heartbeat used for this oracle is only 24 hours https://data.chain.link/ethereum/mainnet/crypto-eth/steth-eth
In this situation, because the heartbeat in the `PriceFeed.sol` is greater than it should, there could be cases where Chainlink is frozen and prices are stale, but because the heartbeat used are bigger, the codebase will take the price as recent and valid, which could lead to problems due to stale pricing. To be more precise, there will be a window of 20 minutes in the case of ETH/BTC and 1 hour for STETH/ETH where prices could be in reality stale, but taken as accurate prices by the codebase.
## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use the recommended heartbeat used also by Chainlink, instead of 1 hour and 20 minutes use only 1 hour and instead of 25 hours use only 24 hours, so the check for stale prices are accurate.

description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/8b518196629faa37eae39736837b24926fd3c07c/smart-contracts/RandomizerRNG.sol#L49


# Vulnerability details



## Impact
arrng-oracle.eth and arrng-captain.eth has the power to set the token hash exactly to their choosing.

## Proof of concept
When a token is minted from a collection which uses RandomizerRNG, RandomizerRNG is called which calls `ArrngController.requestRandomWords()` to get randomness. A callback is expected from (and restricted to) the ArrngController to `ArrnConsumer.receiveRandomness(id, numbers)` which calls
```solidity
function fulfillRandomWords(uint256 id, uint256[] memory numbers) internal override {
    gencoreContract.setTokenHash(tokenIdToCollection[requestToToken[id]], requestToToken[id], bytes32(abi.encodePacked(numbers,requestToToken[id])));
}
```
This sets the token hash to `numbers`.

The callback is initiated by `oracleAddress`, which is currently set to arrng-oracle.eth, in its call to [`ArrngController.serveRandomness()`](https://github.com/arrng/arrng-contracts/blob/117d2eadc55eaabb5bea58396dbc8f421d735fd5/contracts/controller/ArrngController.sol#L474-L508). arrng-oracle.eth is an EOA which provides no guarantees for trust, and he may thus decide to call the callback with arbitrary values. 

He is supposed to provide randomness from and signed by random.org. But this signature is not verified on-chain but can only be optionally and manually verified in retrospect. There is thus nothing preventing arrng-oracle.eth from choosing `numbers` himself. He can thus buy a token and be in full control of which token hash it gets.

The owner, currently arrng-captain.eth, of ArrngController can [set the `oracleAddress`](https://github.com/arrng/arrng-contracts/blob/117d2eadc55eaabb5bea58396dbc8f421d735fd5/contracts/controller/ArrngController.sol#L130-L134), so he can also perform this attack.

## Recommended mitigation steps
The only way arrng.io could even begin to be trusted is if the signature was verified on-chain. This would be costly and complicated to implement, and even then random.org is not completely trustworthy either. arrng.io is simply not a good source of randomness and should not be used. It also seems more expensive than Chainlink VRF, (0.0062 ETH vs. ~0.7 LINK, i.e. \$12.77 vs. ~\$11), so there is no compelling reason not to use Chainlink VRF instead.

description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/8b518196629faa37eae39736837b24926fd3c07c/smart-contracts/NextGenCore.sol#L227-L232
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/8b518196629faa37eae39736837b24926fd3c07c/smart-contracts/RandomizerVRF.sol#L71-L75
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/8b518196629faa37eae39736837b24926fd3c07c/smart-contracts/RandomizerVRF.sol#L52-L63
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/8b518196629faa37eae39736837b24926fd3c07c/smart-contracts/ERC721.sol#L245-L251
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/8b518196629faa37eae39736837b24926fd3c07c/smart-contracts/RandomizerVRF.sol#L65-L68


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Because the user can send a lot of request to the `VRF Coordinator` of Chainlink to generate randomness, anyone can consume all the LINK tokens allowed by the team to pay the requests and also pre-generate the hash token of a token before it's minted. This break the randomness generation of the tokens/NFT guarantee by the protocol.

## Proof of Concept

On the `NextGenCore` contract, the `_mintProcessing()` internal functions is called each time a token is minted by the protocol with `mint()`, `burnToMint()` and `airDropTokens()`.

```solidity
    function _mintProcessing(uint256 _mintIndex, address _recipient, string memory _tokenData, uint256 _collectionID, uint256 _saltfun_o) internal {
        tokenData[_mintIndex] = _tokenData;
        collectionAdditionalData[_collectionID].randomizer.calculateTokenHash(_collectionID, _mintIndex, _saltfun_o);
        tokenIdsToCollectionIds[_mintIndex] = _collectionID;
        _safeMint(_recipient, _mintIndex);
    }
```
The protocol can use 3 differents types of contracts to generate randomness, here we use `RandomizerVRF` contract which use Chainlink.  We can see the function call `calculateTokenHash()` on the randomizer contract to generate the token hash.
The `RandomizerVRF` function work like this: 
```solidity
    function calculateTokenHash(uint256 _collectionID, uint256 _mintIndex, uint256 _saltfun_o) public {
        require(msg.sender == gencore);
        tokenIdToCollection[_mintIndex] = _collectionID;
        requestRandomWords(_mintIndex);
    }

    function requestRandomWords(uint256 tokenid) public {
        require(msg.sender == gencore);
        uint256 requestId = COORDINATOR.requestRandomWords(
            keyHash,
            s_subscriptionId,
            requestConfirmations,
            callbackGasLimit,  
            numWords
        );
        tokenToRequest[tokenid] = requestId;
        requestToToken[requestId] = tokenid;
    }
```
Like it's well explained in the Chainlink documentations:  
https://docs.chain.link/vrf/v2/subscription#how-vrf-processes-your-request

>   How VRF processes your request
    After you submit your request, it is processed using the Request & Receive Data cycle. The VRF coordinator processes the request and determines the final charge to your subscription using the following steps: 
 1) The VRF coordinator emits an event.
 2) The VRF service picks up the event and waits for the specified number of block confirmations to respond back to the VRF coordinator with the random values and a proof (requestConfirmations).
 3) The VRF coordinator verifies the proof on-chain, then it calls back the consuming contract fulfillRandomWords function.



Chainlink VRFCoordinatorV2 is called with `requestRandomWords()` and emits a random request. After `requestConfirmations` blocks, an oracle VRF node replies to the coordinator with a random word, which supplies the random to the requesting contract via `fulfillRandomWords()` callback.
Interesting things is when the call `COORDINATOR.requestRandomWords()` is executed, an event is emitted and the request is processing. But if the minting process revert after the call to the `VRF Coordinator`, the request is sended but all the state revert in the contract.
A user can maliciously revert the transaction by trying to send the token to a contract that doesn't implement the `onERC721Received()` method and revert the `_safeMint` method.
Therefore a user can send a big amount of transactions to the `VRF Coordinator` for the same `tokenId` without the token being minted. It causes multiples problems.

- Firstly, the team have to send a decent amount of LINK tokens to guarantee the request can be executed:
https://docs.chain.link/vrf/v2/subscription#minimum-subscription-balance

>   Each subscription must maintain a minimum balance to fund requests from consuming contracts. 
    This minimum balance requirement serves as a buffer against gas volatility by ensuring that all your requests have more than enough funding to go through. If your balance is below the minimum, your requests remain pending for up to 24 hours before they expire. After you add sufficient LINK to a subscription, pending requests automatically process as long as they have not expired.

A user can send a big number of transactions to consume all the LINK balance of the team account in a very little amount of time because a request can be executed in 3 blocks, (`uint16 public requestConfirmations = 3`), less than 5 minutes.

- Secondly the token hash can be set on the next token to be minted before it's minted. A user send a transaction that revert intentionally and the tokenHash is setted in the `NextGenCore` contract by the `fulfillRandomWords()` callback. Now user can calculate the output of the next token with the artist script and broke the randomness of the token generation.

```solidity
    function fulfillRandomWords(uint256 _requestId, uint256[] memory _randomWords) internal override {
        gencoreContract.setTokenHash(tokenIdToCollection[requestToToken[_requestId]], requestToToken[_requestId], bytes32(abi.encodePacked(_randomWords,requestToToken[_requestId])));
        emit RequestFulfilled(_requestId, _randomWords);
    }
```

# Notes

I think this issue can be considered as High because the randomness of the token generation can be broken by anyone in simple way. And a malicious user can force the team to spend all their availables LINK tokens to request useless random transactions. 

## Tools Used

Manual Review, Chainlink Docs

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Like it's explained in the Security Considerations of the Chainlink VRF docs, you have to respect the procces explained:
https://docs.chain.link/vrf/v2/security#dont-accept-bidsbetsinputs-after-you-have-made-a-randomness-request

>   Consider the example of a contract that mints a random NFT in response to a user's actions.

    The contract should:

    1. Record whatever actions of the user may affect the generated NFT.
    2. Stop accepting further user actions that might affect the generated NFT and issue a randomness request.
    3. On randomness fulfillment, mint the NFT.
   
    Generally speaking, whenever an outcome in your contract depends on some user-supplied inputs and randomness, the contract should not accept any additional user-supplied inputs after it submits the randomness request.

    Otherwise, the cryptoeconomic security properties may be violated by an attacker that can rewrite the chain.

You can decide to call the `_safeMint` function on the `fulfillRandomWords()` callback to asure the token is not minted with zero token hash.
Also create for example a `tokenToRequest[status]` that will be set to false or true to check the status of the requests and make the correct verification that a token can be minted. And add an Admin function to potentially unblock the situation if the `fulfillRandomWords()` can't be executed caused by lack of funds.

It's an example and implement a solution without introduce new bugs needs to be discussed.
If I can help, I'll be glad to do so.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The call to generate randomness will fail in times of high gas price on Eth mainnet due to incorrect hardcoded usage of callbackGasLimit of 40000 and it will not provide random values to the functions calling it but the protocol will lose the link tokens used for randomness requested even though there were no random values provided.

## Proof of Concept
Callback gas is the amount of gas used for the callback request that returns your requested random values. The maximum allowed `callbackGasLimit` value for the requests is decided by the network the contract is being deployed to in this case it is Eth mainnet. Because the VRF v2 Wrapper adds an overhead, our `callbackGasLimit` must not exceed `maxGasLimit - wrapperGasOverhead`.

```solidity
  uint32 public callbackGasLimit = 40000;
```
According to the [Docs of chainlink](https://docs.chain.link/vrf/v2/direct-funding/examples/get-a-random-number#analyzing-the-contract)
 The limit for how much gas to use for the callback request to your contract's `fulfillRandomWords()` function. It must be less than the `maxGasLimit` limit on the coordinator contract minus the `wrapperGasOverhead`. Adjust this value for larger requests depending on how your `fulfillRandomWords()`function processes and stores the received random values. If the `callbackGasLimit` is not sufficient, the callback will fail and your consuming contract is still charged for the work done to generate your requested random values.

```solidity
        );
        tokenToRequest[tokenid] = requestId;
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When an NFT is minted, its TokenHash is generated by using a randomNumber as a salt from some Random Number Generator services like ChainLink VRF and ARRNG. However, there is no guarantee that ARRNG will always fulfill requests for a random number; it can revert sometimes for various reasons. If the request fails to generate a random number, our `receiveRandomness` function won't be called, which, in turn, won't set the token hash for that NFT. This issue will affect art generation, making the generated art look the same because the token hash remains 0.

## Proof of Concept
1) When the [`calculateTokenHash`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/8b518196629faa37eae39736837b24926fd3c07c/smart-contracts/RandomizerRNG.sol#L53) function is called to calculate and set the token hash upon NFT minting.

3) When the ARRNG contract tries to [serveRandomness](https://github.com/arrng/arrng-contracts/blob/117d2eadc55eaabb5bea58396dbc8f421d735fd5/contracts/controller/ArrngController.sol#L474), it can result in [failure](https://github.com/arrng/arrng-contracts/blob/117d2eadc55eaabb5bea58396dbc8f421d735fd5/contracts/controller/ArrngController.sol#L501).

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If the VRF request fails, the NFT token hash will be unable to be set and the user will have paid minting fees for a dud NFT. This could happen the oracle becomes permanently inactive, or an insufficient subscription LINK balance results in a reverted callback and the oracle not re-submitting the failed callback.
## Proof of Concept
The VRF callback `fulfillRandomWords()` is implemented in the `RandomizerVRF` contract; this function is relied upon to set the random hashes of NFTs. See below:
```solidity
    function rawFulfillRandomWords(uint256 requestId, uint256[] memory randomWords) external { // Called by VRF oracle. This function is in VRFConsumerBaseV2
        if (msg.sender != vrfCoordinator) {
        revert OnlyCoordinatorCanFulfill(msg.sender, vrfCoordinator);
        }
        fulfillRandomWords(requestId, randomWords);
    }
```
```solidity
    function fulfillRandomWords(uint256 _requestId, uint256[] memory _randomWords) internal override { // RandomizerVRF's implementation
        gencoreContract.setTokenHash(tokenIdToCollection[requestToToken[_requestId]], requestToToken[_requestId], bytes32(abi.encodePacked(_randomWords,requestToToken[_requestId])));
        emit RequestFulfilled(_requestId, _randomWords);
    }
```
If `fulfillRandomWords` is never called for an NFT, then the random hash of the NFT will be forever zero. As mentioned, this can happen if the oracle shuts down permanently or if the oracle's randomness providing tx fails for whatever reason and the oracle doesn't resubmit the failed tx.
## Recommended Mitigation
Allow the NFT owner and/or contract admin to re-request randomness for a token if the hash is zero and it's been some time since the last request for randomness. `NextGenCore.setTokenHash()` reverts if the hash is nonzero, so this fix will not enable an already-set token hash to be changed.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The lack of slippage and deadline protection mechanisms in the `ERC20TokenEmitter.buyToken()`, operating under a Continuous Variable Rate Gradual Dutch Auction (VRGDAC) model, poses a moderate to high risk. This risk primarily stems from the potential financial loss or unexpected outcomes for users due to the volatile and dynamic pricing nature of the VRGDAC system. In a blockchain environment, where transaction times can be unpredictable and chain reorganizations (reorgs) are possible, the absence of these protections can lead to scenarios where users receive a significantly different amount of tokens than expected or their transactions are executed at an inopportune time. This could result in reduced trust and reliability in the system, potentially impacting its adoption and usage.

## Proof of Concept
1. **Volatility of Token Pricing**: Given the VRGDAC model's time-sensitive pricing, the price at which a user initiates a transaction might significantly differ from the execution price. Specifically, if the emission is ahead of schedule, the price increases exponentially. This can be especially problematic in networks with high congestion or variable transaction times.

2. **Chain Reorgs Impact**: In the event of a chain reorg (Base and Optimism L2s), transactions might be rolled back or altered. Since the VRGDAC price depends on the specific block time and the history of sales up to that point, a reorg could lead to a transaction being executed with a less favorable token amount.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-revolutionprotocol/blob/main/packages/revolution/src/ERC20TokenEmitter.sol#L152-L156

```solidity
    function buyToken(
        address[] calldata addresses,
        uint[] calldata basisPointSplits,
        ProtocolRewardAddresses calldata protocolRewardsRecipients
    ) public payable nonReentrant whenNotPaused returns (uint256 tokensSoldWad) {
```
3. **User Experience and Financial Risk**: Users without the ability to set a maximum slippage limit are exposed to higher financial risks, potentially leading to transactions that result in considerable losses or unanticipated outcomes on the returned `tokensSoldWad`.

Here's a common instance entailed when `AuctionHouse._settleAuction()` externally calls `erc20TokenEmitter.buyToken()`:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-revolutionprotocol/blob/main/packages/revolution/src/AuctionHouse.sol#L398-L409

```solidity
                //Buy token from ERC20TokenEmitter for all the creators
                if (creatorsShare > ethPaidToCreators) {
                    creatorTokensEmitted = erc20TokenEmitter.buyToken{ value: creatorsShare - ethPaidToCreators }(
                        vrgdaReceivers,
                        vrgdaSplits,
                        IERC20TokenEmitter.ProtocolRewardAddresses({
                            builder: address(0),
                            purchaseReferral: address(0),
                            deployer: deployer
                        })
                    );
                }
```
It's understandable zero slippage may be entailed here so that `AuctionHouse._settleAuction()`  will not revert due to minimum `creatorTokensEmitted` not fulfilled. But the slippage option should be extended to all other users buying the tokens directly. 

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. **Implement Slippage Protection**: Introduce a parameter in the buyToken function allowing users to specify a maximum acceptable slippage percentage. The contract should then ensure that the price at execution does not deviate beyond this limit from the price at initiation.

2. **Introduce Deadline Protection**: Add a deadline parameter to transactions, ensuring they are only valid until a specific block time or timestamp. If the transaction is not processed by this deadline, it fails, preventing execution at an unexpected or unfavorable time.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

If the project is just started, a malicious user can make the `_totalSupply` and `_totalShares` imbalance significantly by providing fake income. By doing so, later, when innocent users deposit and mint, the malicious user can steal protocol's stETH without burning any share. Moreover, the protocol's income can be stolen as well.

## Proof of Concept

Suppose nothing is deposited in the protocol (it is day 0).

Bob (a malicious user) deposits $1000 worth of ether (equal to 1 ETH, assuming ETH price is $1000) to mint `200e18 + 1` eUSD. The state will be:
 - `shares[Bob] = 200e18 + 1`
 - `_totalShares = 200e18 + 1`
 - `_totalSupply = 200e18 + 1`
 - `borrowed[Bob] = 200e18 + 1`
 - `poolTotalEUSDCirculation = 200e18 + 1`
 - `depositAsset[Bob] = 1e18`
 - `totalDepositedAsset = 1e18`
 - `stETH.balanceOf(protocol) = 1e18`
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L37

Then, Bob transfers directly `0.2stETH` (worth $200) to the protocol. By doing so, Bob is providing a fake excess income in the protocol. So, the state will be:
 - `shares[Bob] = 200e18 + 1`
 - `_totalShares = 200e18 + 1`
 - `_totalSupply = 200e18 + 1`
 - `borrowed[Bob] = 200e18 + 1`
 - `poolTotalEUSDCirculation = 200e18 + 1`
 - `depositAsset[Bob] = 1e18`
 - `totalDepositedAsset = 1e18`
 - `stETH.balanceOf(protocol) = 1e18 + 2e17`

Then, Bob calls `excessIncomeDistribution` to buy this excess income. As you see in line 63, the `excessIncome` is equal to the difference of `stETH.balanceOf(protocol)` and `totalDepositedAsset`. So, the `excessAmount = 2e17`.
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L63

Then, in line 66, this amount `2e17` is converted to eUSD amount based on the price of stETH. Since, we assumed  ETH is $1000, we have:
```
uint256 payAmount = (((realAmount * getAssetPrice()) / 1e18) * getDutchAuctionDiscountPrice()) / 10000 = 2e17 * 1000e18 / 1e18 = 200e18
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L66C9-L66C112

Since the protocol is just started, there is no `feeStored`, so the income is equal to zero.
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L68

In line 75, we have: 
```
uint256 sharesAmount = _EUSDAmount.mul(_totalShares).div(totalMintedEUSD) = 200e18 * (200e18 + 1) / (200e18 + 1) = 200e18
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L75C13-L75C35

In line 81, this amount of `sharesAmount` will be burned from Bob, and then in line 93, `2e17` stETH will be transferred to Bob. So, the state will be:
 - `shares[Bob] = 200e18 + 1 - 200e18 = 1`
 - `_totalShares = 200e18 + 1 - 200e18 = 1`
 - `_totalSupply = 200e18 + 1`
 - `borrowed[Bob] = 200e18 + 1`
 - `poolTotalEUSDCirculation = 200e18 + 1`
 - `depositAsset[Bob] = 1e18`
 - `totalDepositedAsset = 1e18`
 - `stETH.balanceOf(protocol) = 1e18 + 2e17 - 2e17 = 1e18`
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L81
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L93

**Please note** that currently we have `_totalSupply = 200e18 + 1` and `_totalShares = 1`.

Suppose, Alice (an innocent user) deposits 10ETH, and mints 4000e18 eUSD. So, the amount of shares minted to Alice will be:
```
sharesAmount = _EUSDAmount.mul(_totalShares).div(totalMintedEUSD) = 4000e18 * 1 / (200e18 + 1) = 19
```
So, the state will be:
 - `shares[Bob] = 1`
 - `_totalShares = 1 + 19 = 20`
 - `_totalSupply = 200e18 + 1 + 4000e18 = 4200e18 + 1`
 - `borrowed[Bob] = 200e18 + 1`
 - `poolTotalEUSDCirculation = 200e18 + 1 + 4000e18 = 4200e18 + 1`
 - `depositAsset[Bob] = 1e18`
 - `totalDepositedAsset = 1e18 + 10e18 = 11e18`
 - `stETH.balanceOf(protocol) = 1e18 + 10e18 = 11e18`
 - `shares[Alice] = 19`
 - `borrowed[Alice] = 4000e18`
 - `depositAsset[Alice] = 10e18`

Now, different issues can happen leading to loss/steal of funds:

 - **First Scenario:** If Alice is a provider, Bob can redeem eUSD multiple of times to receive stETH without burning any share by calling `rigidRedemption`. To be more accurate, Bob should call this function with `eusdAmount` as parameter equal to `_totalSupply / _totalShares`. For example:
   - first call: `rigidRedemption (Alice, 210e18)`, so we will have:
      - `shares[Bob] = 1`
      - `_totalShares  = 20`
      - `_totalSupply = 4200e18 + 1 - 210e18 = 3990e18 + 1`
      - `borrowed[Bob] = 200e18 + 1`
      - `poolTotalEUSDCirculation = 4200e18 + 1 - 210e18 = 3990e18 + 1`
      - `depositAsset[Bob] = 1e18`
      - `totalDepositedAsset = 11e18 - 21e16`
      - `stETH.balanceOf(protocol) = 11e18 - 21e16`
      - `shares[Alice] = 19`
      - `borrowed[Alice] = 4000e18 - 210e18 = 3790e18`
      - `depositAsset[Alice] = 10e18 - 21e16`
      Please note that no shares are burned from Bob, because `getSharesByMintedEUSD` returns zero as `210e18 * 20 / (4200e18 + 1) = 0`. It means, Bob receives 0.21 stETH by burning no shares.

   - second call: `rigidRedemption (Alice, 199e18)`, so we will have:
      - `shares[Bob] = 1`
      - `_totalShares  = 20`
      - `_totalSupply = 3990e18 + 1 - 199e18 = 3791e18 + 1`
      - `borrowed[Bob] = 200e18 + 1`
      - `poolTotalEUSDCirculation = 3990e18 + 1 - 199e18 = 3791e18 + 1`
      - `depositAsset[Bob] = 1e18`
      - `totalDepositedAsset = 11e18 - 210e15 - 199e15 = 11e18 - 409e15`
      - `stETH.balanceOf(protocol) = 11e18 - 210e15 - 199e15 = 11e18 - 409e15`
      - `shares[Alice] = 19`
      - `borrowed[Alice] = 3790e18 - 199e18 = 3591e18`
      - `depositAsset[Alice] = 10e18 - 210e15 - 199e15 = 10e18 - 409e15`
      Please note that no shares are burned from Bob, because `getSharesByMintedEUSD` returns zero as `199e18 * 20 / (3990e18 + 1) = 0`. It means, Bob receives 0.199 stETH by burning no shares.

   - third call: `rigidRedemption (Alice, 189e18)`, so we will have:
      - `shares[Bob] = 1`
      - `_totalShares  = 20`
      - `_totalSupply = 3791e18 + 1 - 189e18 = 3602e18 + 1`
      - `borrowed[Bob] = 200e18 + 1`
      - `poolTotalEUSDCirculation = 3791e18 + 1 - 189e18 = 3602e18 + 1`
      - `depositAsset[Bob] = 1e18`
      - `totalDepositedAsset = 11e18 - 409e15 - 189e15 = 11e18 - 598e15`
      - `stETH.balanceOf(protocol) = 11e18 - 409e15 - 189e15 = 11e18 - 598e15`
      - `shares[Alice] = 19`
      - `borrowed[Alice] = 3591e18 - 189e18 = 3402e18`
      - `depositAsset[Alice] = 10e18 - 409e15 - 189e15 = 10e18 - 598e15`
      Please note that no shares are burned from Bob, because `getSharesByMintedEUSD` returns zero as `189e18 * 20 / (3791e18 + 1) = 0`. It means, Bob receives 0.189 stETH by burning no shares.

   So far, by just calling the function `rigidRedemption` three times, Bob received `0.21 + 0.199 + 0.189 = 0.598` stETH (worths $598). If, bob continues calling this function, his gain will increase more and more to the point that `_totalSupply` and `_totalShares` become closer to each other.

   A simple calculation shows that if Bob calls this function 60 times (for sure each time the input parameter should be adjusted based on the `_totalSupply` and `_totalShares`), the state will be:
      - `shares[Bob] = 1`
      - `_totalShares  = 20`
      - `_totalSupply = 203.7e18`
      - `borrowed[Bob] = 200e18 + 1`
      - `poolTotalEUSDCirculation = 203.7e18`
      - `depositAsset[Bob] = 1e18`
      - `totalDepositedAsset = 7e18`
      - `stETH.balanceOf(protocol) = 7e18`
      - `shares[Alice] = 19`
      - `borrowed[Alice] = 3.7e18`
      - `depositAsset[Alice] = 6e18`
   It shows that almost the gain of Bob is 4 stETH (worth $4000).

```
    function getDutchAuctionDiscountPrice() public view returns (uint256 a,uint256 b ) {
```

```
    }
```
Running this demo function gives a = 9867 and b = 10000. This proving our point that in b there is some rounding error/ precision loss. Value a which is derived when multiplication is done before division is the more exact and correct value.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
the `excessIncomeDistribution` function of the `LybraStETHDepositVault` contract (https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L62), sells all the stETH accumulated by the vault over time, to the caller for eUSD. This function applies a discount using a dutch auction model, applying a 1% discount every 30 min after lido's rebase.
Anyone (users, MEV, miners) can look at the mempool, and wait for someone else to call `excessIncomeDistribution`,  than front running it. Making sure to always get the best price possible on sold stETH and neutralizing the whole point of having a dutch auction. 

## Proof of Concept
The `LybraStETHDepositVault` uses the `excessIncomeDistribution(uint256 stETHAmount)` function to sell accumulate stETH and to rebase eUSD.
The price, in eUSD, at which the stETH accumulated will be sold, is computed by `excessIncomeDistribution` using a dutch auction to apply a discount():
```
uint256 payAmount = (((realAmount * getAssetPrice()) / 1e18) * getDutchAuctionDiscountPrice()) / 10000;
```
The dutch auction looks at `block.timestamp`, and use it to compute the amount of discount to apply (since the result will be dived by 10000 in `excessIncomeDistribution`):
```
    function getDutchAuctionDiscountPrice() public view returns (uint256) {
        uint256 time = (block.timestamp - lidoRebaseTime) % 1 days;
        if (time < 30 minutes) return 10000;
        return 10000 - (time / 30 minutes - 1) * 100;
    }
```
(https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L101)

As you can notice by looking at the contract, there isn't any type of front run protection on this auction, which opens up the opportunity for the following scenario:

Step0: Users use the vault normally generating yield over time.
Step1: Alice wants to buy the stETH accumulated at the best price possible, to do so she start observing the mempool 
Step2: Bob sees that there is a good discount on the stETH available and calls excessIncomeDistribution to buy it
Step3: Alice sees Bob bid on the dutch auction, and front runs his request.

With this implementation, a malicious user has no reason to participate regularly to the dutch auction, but they can simply wait for someone else to place a bid, and than decide if they want to front run it or not. Braking the main purpose of an auction.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The contracts for RETH Token and WBETH Token lack the exchangeRatio() function, which will revert any deposit to these Vaults. This omission can have significant consequences for users interacting with these contracts.

## Proof of Concept
Regarding RETH, the provided interface for RocketTokenRETHInterface.sol does not include the required function. Instead, the smart contract should call the getEthValue() function. You can find the interface code at the following location:
https://github.com/rocket-pool/rocketpool/blob/master/contracts/interface/token/RocketTokenRETHInterface.sol#L8

For WBETH, no open source documentation or GitHub repository was found. However, you can verify the code on Etherscan by referring to the provided address: 0x523177fbe442afb70b401d06bb11ec7b8684ecee (proxyContract). The relevant file to inspect is StakedTokenV1.sol#L256.


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To address the issues identified, the following mitigation steps are recommended:

For LybraRETHVault.sol:

Modify the IRETH interface to include the getEthValue() function:
```
interface IRETH {
    function getEthValue(uint256 _rethAmount) external view returns (uint256);  
}
```
Update the getAssetPrice() function in LybraRETHVault.sol as follows:
```
function getAssetPrice() public override returns (uint256) {
    return (_etherPrice() * IRETH(address(collateralAsset)).getEthValue(1e18)) / 1e18;
}
```
For WBETH using the address 0xa2E3356610840701BDf5611a53974510Ae27E2e1:
Change exchangeRatio to exchangeRate in the IWBETH interface:
```
interface IWBETH {
    function exchangeRate() external view returns (uint256);
    function deposit(address referral) external payable;
}
```
Modify the getAssetPrice() function in LybraRETHVault.sol accordingly:
```
function getAssetPrice() public override returns (uint256) {
    return (_etherPrice() * IWBETH(address(collateralAsset)).exchangeRate()) / 1e18;
}
```
It's important to note that while inspecting the WBETH contract, it was observed that the exchangeRate value is derived from an off-chain oracle update, likely sourced from Binance. This information should be taken into account and used with caution when utilizing the function.

## Impact

User can potentially mint more EUSD than allowed if stETH is worth less than ETH, and vice versa.

## Proof of Concept

Firstly, note that `getAssetPrice()` in LybraStETHVaul.sol returns `_etherPrice()`, which is the price of ETH in 18 decimal places.

```
    function getAssetPrice() public override returns (uint256) {
        return (_etherPrice() * IWstETH(address(collateralAsset)).stEthPerToken()) / 1e18;
    }
```

Even though both tokens have a tendency to keep the peg, this hasn't been always the case as it can be seen in this [dashboard](https://dune.com/LidoAnalytical/Curve-ETHstETH). There have been many episodes of market volatility that affected the price of stETH, notably the one in last June when stETH traded at ~0.93 ETH. 

stETH is used to mint EUSD. whenever `_mintEUSD()` is called, `_checkHealth()` will also be called. `_checkHealth()` makes sure that the borrowed amount is less than the safe collateral ratio.

```
    function _checkHealth(address _user, uint256 _assetPrice) internal view {
        if (((depositedAsset[_user] * _assetPrice * 100) / borrowed[_user]) < configurator.getSafeCollateralRatio(address(this))) revert("collateralRatio is Below safeCollateralRatio");
    }
```

Let's look at the calculation of `_checkHealth()`. Assume the following:

1. stETH is worth 95% of ETH.
2. safeCollateralRatio is at 160%
3. ETH price is 1000 USD , and thus stETH is 950 USD
4. User deposits 10 stETH, and attempts to mint 6249 EUSD. 

10 ETH is worth 10000 USD, but 10 stETH is worth 9500 USD. If ETH is assumed to be 1:1 with stETH, the following issue will occur:

```
(Assuming 1:1 ratio)
if (((depositedAsset[_user] * _assetPrice * 100) / borrowed[_user]) < 160e18 ) revert
if (((10e18 * 1000e18 * 100) / 6251e18) < 160e18 ) revert
if (1.600256e20 < 1.6e20) revert

Since 1.600256e18 is greater than 1.6e20, user is allowed to mint 6249 tokens as collateral ratio is 160.002%

(Not 1:1 ratio)
if (((depositedAsset[_user] * _assetPrice * 100) / borrowed[_user]) < 160e18 ) revert
if (((10e18 * 950e18 * 100) / 6251e18) < 160e18 ) revert
if (1.5202432e20 < 1.6e20) revert

Since 1.5202432e20 < 1.6e20, user is not allowed to mint 6249 tokens as collateral ratio is now 152%
```

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Recommend fetching the actual price of stETH using external oracles like Chainlink or fetch price on-chain like using the curve eth/steth pool to derive the steth price in terms of eth.

There is a check indicating that the provider has given the allowance to the Lybra contract or not. 

In the `liquidation`, this check is: 
`require(EUSD.allowance(provider, address(this)) > 0, "provider should authorize to provide liquidation EUSD");`
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/base/LybraEUSDVaultBase.sol#L160C9-L160C119

In the `superLiquidation`, this condition is:
`require(EUSD.allowance(provider, address(this)) >= eusdAmount, "provider should authorize to provide liquidation EUSD");`
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/base/LybraEUSDVaultBase.sol#L197

So, in `liquidation` it is compared to **zero**, while in `superLiquidation` it is compared to **eusdAmount**.

It is not clear in the project that the allowance is supposed to be used as **a limit on the provider's fund to be used for liquidation** or as **a flag that enables an user as a provider or not**.

There are different scenarios that should be noted:

##### First scenario:

During selling excess income for eUSD, the function `excessIncomeDistribution` should be called.
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L62C14-L62C38

In order to pay the eUSD to the protocol to get stETH (excess income), it is necessary to give the allowance to the protocol beforehand. 
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L70
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L85

If an user gives higher allowance (this is highly possible because the user does not know exactly how much eUSD should be transferred as `_newFee()` and `getDutchAuctionDiscountPrice()` returns dynamic values),. then there will be nonzero allowance from the user to the protocol. So, any keeper can use this user as provider (because the allowance of the user is now nonzero) and uses his fund for liquidation.

Even, the keeper can front-run the user between the `approve` tx and `excessIncomeDistribution` tx to use the user as a provider.

In other words, a victim user would like to use the feature of `excessIncomeDistribution`, so he needs to give allowance to the protocol, but he is not aware that giving allowance to the protocol enables him as a provider. So, it will be a clear misuse of victim user's fund in an unexpected/unwanted tx.

Please note that the `transferFrom` is implemented differently as it indicates that if the `trasnferFrom` is called from a vault (which is activated by the DAO), then it is not necessary that `from` has already given allowance to the `spender` (here is the vault). 
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/token/EUSD.sol#L228
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/7b73ef2fbb542b569e182d9abf79be643ca883ee/contracts/lybra/configuration/LybraConfigurator.sol#L109

##### Second scenario:

For example, userA is a provider (i.e. he has given allowance to the protocol), and he has some ETH and 100,000 eUSDC, and he has given allowance of 50,000 eUSDC to the protocol. If userB is under bad collateral rate (for example, he can be liquidated by 60,000), we can liquidate userB:
 - If the condition matches with **liquidation criteria**, we can liquidate 60,000 userB by burning 60,000 eUSD from userA. Because, userA's allowance is higher than zero.
 - If the condition matches with **superLiquidation criteria**, we can superLiquidate 60,000 userB in two steps. First, by burning 50,000 eUSD from userA, and second, by burning 10,000 eUSD from userA. Because, userA's allowance is 50,000.

So, the `eusdAmount` in condition `require(EUSD.allowance(provider, address(this)) >= eusdAmount, "provider should authorize to provide liquidation EUSD");` in `superLiquidation` does not make any limitation.

##### Third scenario:
Let's say userA has some collateral and borrow and has given the allowance to the protocol to be used as a liquidator. Later, he decides to withdraw his collateral by repaying his borrowed amount. Since, during withdrawing (or burning) his allowance is not zeroed, this user has still nonzero allowance to the protocol. If later, the eUSD balance of this user is increased (by any reason, like a simple transfer, or he swapped USDC to eUSD for any economical reason), since the allowance to the protocol is not zeroed before, any keeper can use userA's balance to liquidate other users under bad collateral rate. This can lead to financial loss of userA.
Suppose, userA predicts that eUSD price will increase. So, he swaps USDC to eUSD to hold eUSD, and to sell it later when the price of eUSD is increased. When there are some users who are under bad collateral rate, the keeper can use userA's eUSDC balance to liquidate other users under bad collateral rate. By doing so, userA will lose his eUSD and receives ETH in return (depending on the value of ETH, this can be a big loss to userA). This is a clear way of misusing userA's allowance because userA did not have plan to to be provider anymore.


Please note that in general using allowance of users to enable them as a provider is not a safe action because if any vulnerability leads to the control of the protocol, it is possible to steal the fund of users who have already given allowance to the protocol just to be provider.


## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
There can be some fixes:
 - Using the same condition for both `liquidation` and `superLiquidation` to fix the discrepancy.
 - Defining another variable to be used for being an provider instead of using allowance.
 - Updating allowance if provider's fund is used during liquidation.

description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/5d70170f2c68dbd3f7b8c0c8fd6b0b2218784ea6/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L97-L105


# Vulnerability details



## Impact

The [LybraWstETHVault](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/5d70170f2c68dbd3f7b8c0c8fd6b0b2218784ea6/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.so) contract utilizes block-based time calculations to determine the discount for the issuance of additional tokens using the Dutch auction method. However, this approach may not yield accurate results on chains with varying block times. Specifically, the current implementation does not account for the differences in block times between chains, leading to potentially incorrect discount rates for issuing additional tokens.

For example, let's consider the comparison between Ethereum and Fantom. Ethereum has a block time of 12 seconds, while Fantom has a block time of 0.8 seconds. This significant difference means that the elapsed time since the last rebase will accumulate at a much faster rate on Fantom compared to Ethereum. Consequently, the condition `time < 30 minutes` within the `getDutchAuctionDiscountPrice` function will be satisfied much more quickly on Fantom (~ 15X faster), resulting in different discount rate calculations.

## Proof of Concept

The LybraStETHDepositVault contract contains the [`getDutchAuctionDiscountPrice`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/blob/5d70170f2c68dbd3f7b8c0c8fd6b0b2218784ea6/contracts/lybra/pools/LybraStETHVault.sol#L97-L105) function, which is responsible for calculating the discount rate based on the rebase time using the Dutch auction method. However, the function relies on the `block.timestamp` value without considering the variations in block times on different chains.

```solidity
function getDutchAuctionDiscountPrice() public view returns (uint256) {
    uint256 time = (block.timestamp - lidoRebaseTime) % 1 days;
    if (time < 30 minutes) return 10000;
    return 10000 - (time / 30 minutes - 1) * 100;
}
```

## Tool used

Manual Review

## Recommendation

It is recommended to modify the approach used for time calculations in the `getDutchAuctionDiscountPrice` function to ensure accurate and consistent functionality across different blockchain networks. Consider the following recommendations:

1. Implement a method that calculates the elapsed time based on time passed rather than relying solely on `block.timestamp`. This can be achieved by using an alternative time-tracking mechanism, such as a trusted external oracle or an off-chain time provider.

2. If preferred, adapt the conditional calculations based on the specific characteristics of each chain. Different block times necessitate adjusting the conditionals to reflect the expected time intervals accurately.

### Additional Notes

This report only focuses on the case of fantom for brevity reasons, but the same case is the case in other chains too since say ARB has a block time of ~15seconds which is 25% more than that of eth, which means that the discount would happen slower and on networks with lower block times, the distribution will happen a lot faster.
Key to note that being a pioneer in the space as of version 4.9, OpenZeppelin has [modified](https://blog.openzeppelin.com/introducing-openzeppelin-contracts-v4.9#governor) their governor code to use a clock rather than block numbers, to avoid these sorts of issues, but this still requires that the project [implement](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/governance#token_2) a [clock](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-6372) for each L2.
Lastly the [scoping-details](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-lybra/tree/main#scoping-details) of this contest indicate that it is a multi-chain project.

# Lines of code
