title: Unspent RSR can be stolen
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/reserve-protocol/protocol/blob/27a3472d553b4fa54f896596007765ec91941348/contracts/p1/BackingManager.sol#L176-L182


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `BackingManager.handoutExcessAssets` function sends all rsr that the BackingManager holds to the StRSR contract. This is done so that the rsr which is held by the BackingManager due to seizure from the StRSR contract can be sent back entirely to the StRSR contract. 

Whenever a seizure of rsr occurs the staker balances are zeroed out and new era is started. All unspent rsr sent from BackingManager becomes claimable to new stakers.

```solidity
        if (rsr.balanceOf(address(this)) > 0) {
            // For CEI, this is an interaction "within our system" even though RSR is already live
            IERC20Upgradeable(address(rsr)).safeTransfer(
                address(stRSR), 
                rsr.balanceOf(address(this))
            );
        }
```

This can be used by an attacker to advantageously gain unintended rsr rewards.


## Proof of Concept
Consider this scenario:

 - A seizure of rsr from the StRSR contract occurred because the RToken was under-collateralized.

 - A trade occurred which restored collateralization. However not all rsr were sold by the trade and was returned to the BackingManager.

 - `BackingManager.manageTokens` was invoked which transferred all available rsr to StRSR contract.

 - As due to seizure, all balances of previous stakers were zeroed out, an attacker can immediately become the solo staker in the StRSR contract and reap rsr rewards advantageously.

 - The `PERIOD` value is also reduced to 12 seconds which favours the attacker. As the attacker can reap rewards every 12 seconds.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The protocol should rethink about the use of unspent rsr tokens, ideally they should be distributed on a prorata basis to all previous stakers. 

The newly sent rsr tokens by BackingManager can be excluded from the rewards for a while until sufficient number of new stakers stake again in the StRSR contract.

title: Attacker can cause loss to rToken holders and stakers by running BackingManager._manageTokens before rewards are claimed
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/reserve-protocol/protocol/blob/27a3472d553b4fa54f896596007765ec91941348/contracts/p1/BackingManager.sol#L105-L153


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The assets that back the rTokens are held by the `BackingManager` and can earn rewards.  

The rewards can be claimed via the [`TradingP1.claimRewards`](https://github.com/reserve-protocol/protocol/blob/27a3472d553b4fa54f896596007765ec91941348/contracts/p1/mixins/Trading.sol#L82-L84) and [`TradingP1.claimRewardsSingle`](https://github.com/reserve-protocol/protocol/blob/27a3472d553b4fa54f896596007765ec91941348/contracts/p1/mixins/Trading.sol#L90-L92) function.  

The `BackingManager` inherits from `TradingP1` and therefore the above functions can be used to claim rewards.  

The issue is that the `BackingManager` does not claim rewards as part of its [`_manageTokens`](https://github.com/reserve-protocol/protocol/blob/27a3472d553b4fa54f896596007765ec91941348/contracts/p1/BackingManager.sol#L105-L153) function.  

So recollateralization can occur before rewards have been claimed.  

There exist possibilities how an attacker can exploit this to cause a loss to rToken holders and rsr stakers.  

## Proof of Concept
Let's think about an example for such a scenario:  

Assume that the `RToken` is backed by a considerable amount of `TokenA`

`TokenA` earns rewards but not continuously. Bigger amounts of rewards are paid out periodically. Say 5% rewards every year.  

Assume further that the `RToken` is currently undercollateralized.  

The attacker can now front-run the claiming of rewards and perform recollateralization.  

The recollateralization might now seize `rsr` from stakers or take an unnecessary haircut.  

## Tools Used
VSCode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
I suggest that the `BackingManager._manageTokens` function calls `claimRewards`. Even before it calculates how many baskets it holds:  

```diff
diff --git a/contracts/p1/BackingManager.sol b/contracts/p1/BackingManager.sol
index fc38ce29..e17bb63d 100644
--- a/contracts/p1/BackingManager.sol
+++ b/contracts/p1/BackingManager.sol
@@ -113,6 +113,8 @@ contract BackingManagerP1 is TradingP1, IBackingManager {
         uint48 basketTimestamp = basketHandler.timestamp();
         if (block.timestamp < basketTimestamp + tradingDelay) return;
 
+        this.claimRewards();
+
         uint192 basketsHeld = basketHandler.basketsHeldBy(address(this));
 
         // if (basketHandler.fullyCollateralized())
```

title: StRSR: attacker can steal excess rsr that is returned after seizure
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/reserve-protocol/protocol/blob/27a3472d553b4fa54f896596007765ec91941348/contracts/p1/BackingManager.sol#L176-L182
https://github.com/reserve-protocol/protocol/blob/27a3472d553b4fa54f896596007765ec91941348/contracts/p1/StRSR.sol#L496-L530


# Vulnerability details

**Note:**  
This issue deals with excess `rsr` that was seized from `stRSR` but is returned again.  
The `M-12` issue also deals with excess `rsr`.  

However `M-12` deals with the fact that not all `rsr` is returned to `stRSR`, whereas this issue deals with the fact that an attacker can steal `rsr` once it is returned to `stRSR`.  

So while the issues seem to be similar they in fact are different.  

They are separate issues. So I chose to report this separately with the `NEW` keyword.  

## Impact
`rsr` can be returned to `stRSR` after a seizure if not all seized `rsr` has been necessary to regain full collateralization.  

This happens in the [`BackingManger.handoutExcessAssets`](https://github.com/reserve-protocol/protocol/blob/27a3472d553b4fa54f896596007765ec91941348/contracts/p1/BackingManager.sol#L176-L182) function.  

This excess `rsr` is then paid out to ALL stakers just like regular `rsr` rewards using the [`StRSR._payoutRewards`](https://github.com/reserve-protocol/protocol/blob/27a3472d553b4fa54f896596007765ec91941348/contracts/p1/StRSR.sol#L496-L530) function.  

This is unfair. An attacker can abuse this behavior and stake `rsr` to profit from the returned `rsr` which is used to appreciate his `stRSR`.  

It would be fair if the `rsr` was returned only to the users that had staked when the seizure occurred.  

## Proof of Concept
Think of the following scenario:  

1. There are currently 100 stakers with an equal share of the `1000 rsr` total that is currently in the `stRSR` contract.  
2. A seizure occurs and `500 rsr` are seized.
3. Not all `rsr` is sold and some (say `50 rsr`) is returned to `StRSR`
4. The attacker can front-run the transaction that returns the `rsr` and become a staker himself
5. The attacker will profit from the returned `rsr` once it is paid out as reward. Say the attacker stakes `100 rsr`. He now owns a share of `100 rsr / (500 rsr + 100 rsr) = 20%`. This means he will also get `20%` of the `50 rsr` that are paid out as rewards.  

## Tools Used
VSCode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ideally, as I said above, the `rsr` should be returned only to the users that had staked when the seizure occurred.  

With the current architecture of the `stRSR` contract this is not possible. There is no way to differentiate between stakers.  

Also the scenario described is an edge and relies on a seizure to occur and `rsr` to be returned.  

It seems unrealistic that `10%` of the seized `rsr` is returned again. I think a number like `1% - 5%` is more realistic.  

But still if the amount of `rsr` that is seized is big enough, `1% - 5%` can be a significant amount in terms of dollar value.  

I estimate this to be `Medium` severity since an attacker can profit at the expense of other stakers and this behavior will decrease the willingness of users to stake as the risk of losing funds is increased.  

This severly damages the incentives involved with staking. Stakers are incentivized to wait for seizures to occur and only then stake as they might profit from returned `rsr`.  

I encourage the sponsor to further assess if there is a better way to return excess `rsr`.

title: Early attacker can DOS rToken issuance
Gas is not consumed when precompile method fail, allowing resource consumption related DOS
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-11-nibiru/blob/main/x/evm/precompile/funtoken.go#L79-L84
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-11-nibiru/blob/main/x/evm/precompile/wasm.go#L71-L79
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-11-nibiru/blob/main/x/evm/precompile/oracle.go#L60-L64


# Vulnerability details

## Finding description and impact

When a precompile method fails (e.g., due to an error), **gas is not consumed** as the method returns early before invoking the gas consumption logic. This issue affects all three precompiles in the system:

- **FunToken**
- **Wasm**
- **Oracle**

The lack of gas consumption on failure allows attackers to perform denial-of-service (DoS) attacks by exploiting the failure conditions to consume excessive resources without paying for them. The code snippet below demonstrates the issue:

```go
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}

// Gas consumed by a local gas meter
contract.UseGas(startResult.CacheCtx.GasMeter().GasConsumed())
```

### Impact:
1. Resource Consumption without Gas Payment: Since gas is not consumed on failure, an attacker can repeatedly trigger precompile failures, consuming large amounts of resources without the associated cost.
2. Potential DoS Attack: This can lead to a DoS attack, where an attacker fills the block with failed precompile executions, causing network slowdowns, failures, or even halting the chain.
3. Block Gas Limit Exploitation: Before the precompile.Run method is called, a small amount of requiredGas is consumed. However, once this is consumed, attackers can continue to use gas at no cost, potentially exhausting the block gas limit.

## Proof of Concept
1. Create an EVM Contract: Design an EVM contract that calls the `wasm.execute` function repeatedly, up to the `maxMultistoreCacheCount` (10) times.
2. Trigger the DoS: Call the contract with a transaction that uses a large amount of gas limit.
3. Exploit the Failure: In the `wasm.execute` function, consume almost all of the available gas and then revert the transaction. This will allow the attacker to consume gas without paying for it, leveraging the bug in the precompile failure handling.

## Recommended mitigation steps

Use gas before returning the `err`

```go
// Gas consumed by a local gas meter
contract.UseGas(startResult.CacheCtx.GasMeter().GasConsumed())

if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
```

title: Inconsistent State Management: EthereumTx StateDB Overriding CallContract Results
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-11-nibiru/blob/main/x/evm/statedb/statedb.go#L515-L586


# Vulnerability details

## Finding Description and Impact

When a precompile is invoked, the context (`ctx`) is cached, and the state database (`statedb`) commits to this cache, ensuring that precompiles operate with the most up-to-date context and data. During the execution of the precompile, the context can be modified, but these changes are not fully reflected in the state database, except for bank-related modifications. 

```go
func (s *StateDB) Commit() error {
	if s.writeToCommitCtxFromCacheCtx != nil {
		s.writeToCommitCtxFromCacheCtx()
	}
	return s.commitCtx(s.GetEvmTxContext())
}
```

The snippet above shows that at the end of the transaction, the `evmTxCtx` is updated to the cached context (`cachedCtx`) before the state changes are committed by the `statedb.commitCtx`. However, the issue arises because **EvmState and Account modifications made within `cachedCtx` can be overwritten when `statedb.commitCtx` commits the state changes**. This creates a situation where certain state changes, particularly those made by precompiles like FunToken, can be lost or corrupted.

For example, the **FunToken precompile** may call `CallContract` and modify `EvmState`'s `AccState` after the account state object has been added to the `statedb` and dirtied.

### Impact
1. **Unlimited Token Minting**: The state inconsistencies could allow the minting of unlimited FunTokens, as state changes made during precompile execution may be overwritten.
2. **State Corruption**: The precompile could corrupt the state of any contract by exploiting the `statedb`'s lack of awareness of the modifications made during precompile execution.
3. **Malicious Contract Exploits**: An attacker could create a malicious ERC20 token, which, when added to FunToken, could leverage the `MaliciousERC20.transfer` method as a callback to perform arbitrary operations on any contract, including state manipulation.
4. **Locking Factories**: A lot of factories use create which depends on their nonce being incremented in sequence. If a nonce is reused, the transaction would fail because there's already a contract where they want to deploy.

## Proof of Concept

* CreateFunToken: Add Nibi, or any valuable coin to FunToken
* ConvertCoinToEvm: Convert Nibi to ERC20
* Create eth tx that performs this in the smart contract
    * transfer WEI to add object to statedb
    * Convert X ERC20 to Nibi through `FunToken.sendToBank`. It would reduce balanceOf contract by X amount, and mint X Nibi coins to the contract.
* At the End of EthereumTx, statedb would commit the balanceOf contract to the initial balance before `FunToken.sendToBank` 

The transfer to add object to statedb can also be done after Precompile is called because `statedb` would get account and object from `evmTxCtx` which is lagging `cachedCtx`

## Recommended mitigation steps

Make sure EthereumTx.statedb knows what CallContracts in Precompile have done. And it has to work well when reverts occur.

title: IOracle.queryExchangeRate returns incorrect blockTimeMs
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-11-nibiru/blob/8ed91a036f664b421182e183f19f6cef1a4e28ea/x/evm/precompile/oracle.go#L92


# Vulnerability details

The IOracle.queryExchangeRate offers the following lookup functionality, in analogy to other oracles like Chainlinks':

```Solidity
    /// @notice Queries the dated exchange rate for a given pair
    /// @param pair The asset pair to query. For example, "ubtc:uusd" is the
    /// USD price of BTC and "unibi:uusd" is the USD price of NIBI.
    /// @return price The exchange rate for the given pair
    /// @return blockTimeMs The block time in milliseconds when the price was
    /// last updated
    /// @return blockHeight The block height when the price was last updated
    /// @dev This function is view-only and does not modify state.
    function queryExchangeRate(
        string memory pair
    ) external view returns (uint256 price, uint64 blockTimeMs, uint64 blockHeight);
```

If we focus on the `blockTimeMs` returned value, this is meant to correspond to the time when the price was last updated
and, in analogy to how Chainlink oracles are typically used, is most likely to be used in staleness checks.

If we see how this is implemented, we see that values are passed through from OracleKeeper (L92):

```go
File: oracle.go
78: func (p precompileOracle) queryExchangeRate(
79: 	ctx sdk.Context,
80: 	method *gethabi.Method,
81: 	args []any,
82: ) (bz []byte, err error) {
83: 	pair, err := p.parseQueryExchangeRateArgs(args)
84: 	if err != nil {
85: 		return nil, err
86: 	}
87: 	assetPair, err := asset.TryNewPair(pair)
88: 	if err != nil {
89: 		return nil, err
90: 	}
91: 
92: 	price, blockTime, blockHeight, err := p.oracleKeeper.GetDatedExchangeRate(ctx, assetPair)
93: 	if err != nil {
94: 		return nil, err
95: 	}
96: 
97: 	return method.Outputs.Pack(price.BigInt(), uint64(blockTime), blockHeight)
98: }
```

However, the `blockTime` returned by `oracleKeeper.GetDatedExchangeRate` corresponds to the "current" block time and
therefore does not correspond to what should be returned by the precompile, that is the block time of the last price update.

The impact of this misalignment is quite severe, because since the returned value is the timestamp returned is always that
of the current block, the price will always look as freshly set when validated against `blockTime`, which is the most
common validation. Consequently, downstream contracts will likely always pass staleness checks on potentially extremely old prices.

## Proof of Concept
A simple coded PoC for this issue consists of updating the `TestOracle_HappyPath` test in 
`x/evm/precompile/oracle_test.go` to simulate a precompile call at a later block than that of the price update - 
changing L66 as follows will cause the test to fail:

```go
File: x/evm/precompile/oracle_test.go
57: func (s *OracleSuite) TestOracle_HappyPath() {
58: 	deps := evmtest.NewTestDeps()
59: 
60: 	s.T().Log("Query exchange rate")
61: 	{
62: 		deps.Ctx = deps.Ctx.WithBlockTime(time.Unix(69, 420)).WithBlockHeight(69)
63: 		deps.App.OracleKeeper.SetPrice(deps.Ctx, "unibi:uusd", sdk.MustNewDecFromStr("0.067"))
64: 
65: 		resp, err := deps.EvmKeeper.CallContract(
66: 			deps.Ctx.WithBlockTime(deps.Ctx.BlockTime().Add(10*time.Second)), //  @audit query 10 seconds later
67: 			embeds.SmartContract_Oracle.ABI,
68: 			deps.Sender.EthAddr,
69: 			&precompile.PrecompileAddr_Oracle,
70: 			false,
71: 			OracleGasLimitQuery,
72: 			"queryExchangeRate",
73: 			"unibi:uusd",
74: 		)
75: 		s.NoError(err)
76: 
77: 		// Check the response
78: 		out, err := embeds.SmartContract_Oracle.ABI.Unpack(string(precompile.OracleMethod_queryExchangeRate), resp.Ret)
79: 		s.NoError(err)
80: 
81: 		// Check the response
82: 		s.Equal(out[0].(*big.Int), big.NewInt(67000000000000000))
83: 		s.Equal(out[1].(uint64), uint64(69000))
84: 		s.Equal(out[2].(uint64), uint64(69))
85: 	}
86: }
```

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider maintaining and querying a lookup table (height to time) for returning the right `blockTime` instead of 
relying on the value passed by `GetDatedExchangeRate`.

title: Invalid settlement handlers can process received cross-chain messages and callbacks in ChakraSettlement.sol
`ChakraSettlement::receive_cross_chain_callback` is Vulnerable to DoS Through Nonce Manipulation and Will Always Revert
receive_cross_chain_callback in handler contract will revert because of inconsistent txid in handler contract and settlement contract in some case
Anyone can cause a permanent DoS of the execution of the solidity callback function of any address. And `created_tx` instances on cairo's handler will always be desynced
It is possible to prevent executing the `receive_cross_chain_callback` in the solidity handler
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/main/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L294


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability description
The `receive_cross_chain_callback` settlement function is intended to only be called by validators, however it is open for everyone but it must assert that the signatures provided match with the message provided in the function:
```
    function receive_cross_chain_callback(
        uint256 txid,
        string memory from_chain,
        uint256 from_handler,
        address to_handler,
        CrossChainMsgStatus status,
        uint8 sign_type,
        bytes calldata signatures
    ) external {
        verifySignature(
            txid,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            status,
            sign_type,
            signatures
        );
        processCrossChainCallback(
            txid,
            from_chain,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            status,
            sign_type,
            signatures
        );
        emitCrossChainResult(txid);
    }
```
Someone can think it is save because even though someone frontruns the transaction and tries to change any parameter it will fail because the message with the parameters has been signed by offchain validators and it must comply that the parameters match. However not all parameters are hashed in the signed message. That is really important because someone can change it and the signatures will still pass.

In this case, the particular parameter that is not signed in the message is the `from_chain` parameter.
```
    function verifySignature(
        uint256 txid,
        uint256 from_handler,
        address to_handler,
        CrossChainMsgStatus status,
        uint8 sign_type,
        bytes calldata signatures
    ) internal view {
        bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
            abi.encodePacked(txid, from_handler, to_handler, status)
        );

        require(
            signature_verifier.verify(message_hash, signatures, sign_type),
            "Invalid signature"
        );
    }
```

That means that a message that has been signed with the other data can be provided to the function with any arbitrary `from_chain` and it will pass the signature check.

## Proof of concept
1. A user initiates an ERC20 MintBurn type
2. Tokens are minted in the destination chain
3. The validator submits the data in the mempool to call the callback function
4. A malicious user monitors it and frontruns the function call providing the exact same parameters but changing the `from_chain` parameter to any arbitrary string
5. The settlement calls the handler and it returns false because it will not have whitelisted the handler address on this other invented chain string.
```
        if (is_valid_handler(from_chain, from_handler) == false) {
            return false;
        }
```
6. The end result will be the cross transaction marked as failed when it has minted the tokens in the destination chain and the source chain not being able to burn the tokens.
7. The validators call will fail because the cross transaction has a different state of `PENDING`.
```
        require(
            create_cross_txs[txid].status == CrossChainMsgStatus.Pending,
            "Invalid transaction status"
        );
```



## Impact
The impact of this issue is high because it can be performed by anyone on any message and it prevents executing the logic from the callback function. The current implementation of the callback function in the handler only involves burning tokens but in the future can be more logic that will be skipped. Also the `create_cross_txs` transaction will be marked as failed when in reality the tokens where minted succesfully on the destination chain.


## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add the `from_chain` parameter into the message hashing.
```diff
    function receive_cross_chain_callback(
        uint256 txid,
        string memory from_chain,
        uint256 from_handler,
        address to_handler,
        CrossChainMsgStatus status,
        uint8 sign_type,
        bytes calldata signatures
    ) external {
        verifySignature(
            txid,
++          from_chain,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            status,
            sign_type,
            signatures
        );
        processCrossChainCallback(
            txid,
            from_chain,
            from_handler,
            to_handler,
            status,
            sign_type,
            signatures
        );
        emitCrossChainResult(txid);
    }

    function verifySignature(
        uint256 txid,
++      string calldata from_chain,
        uint256 from_handler,
        address to_handler,
        CrossChainMsgStatus status,
        uint8 sign_type,
        bytes calldata signatures
    ) internal view {
        bytes32 message_hash = keccak256(
--          abi.encodePacked(txid, from_handler, to_handler, status)
++          abi.encodePacked(txid, from_chain, from_handler, to_handler, status)
        );

        require(
            signature_verifier.verify(message_hash, signatures, sign_type),
            "Invalid signature"
        );
    }
```



## Assessed type

DoS

title: wrong created_tx key is used to get wrong created_tx mapping state in receive_cross_chain_callback function because of inconsistent txid in handler contract and settlement contract in some case
description:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L183
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L289
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L138-L165


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If msg_count in handler contract and settlement contract is different, user's message txid is different in handler contract and settlement contract. when `receive_cross_chain_callback` is called, the txid is passed directly from settlement contract to handler contract in receive-callback context. So wrong created_tx key(txid) is used to modify created_tx mapping state and get wrong created_tx mapping state in `receive_cross_chain_callback` function in handler_erc20.cairo.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/handler_erc20.cairo#L183
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/d0d45ae1d26ca1b87034e67180fac07ce9642fd9/cairo/handler/src/settlement.cairo#L289
There are four handler contracts and one settlement contract on one chain. A user can set cross-chain message by arbitrary handler contract depending on the mode.
The txid is calculated using follow ways:
handler contract →
```
           let tx_id = LegacyHash::hash(get_tx_info().unbox().transaction_hash, self.msg_count.read());
```
settlement contract →
```
            let cross_chain_settlement_id = LegacyHash::hash(get_tx_info().unbox().transaction_hash, self.tx_count.read());
```
The method of calculation is the same in handler contract and settlement contract.
However we have four handler contracts and settlement contract. It's very easy to let msg_count in handler contract and settlement contract not equal as long as more than one handler contracts are used.
For example:

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Callbacks can be DOS-ed by a malicious actor.

## Proof of Concept
When a message is send from the handler, a `txid` is computed by hashing the nonce of the sender. This `txid` is recorded as `Pending` in the handler contract. After that, the settlement contract [recomputes](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L118-L133) the hash by using the nonce of the sender based on its own mapping. 

Anyone can repeatedly call [ChakraSettlement.send_cross_chain_msg()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L111-L156) with an arbitrary `fromAddress` and cause the nonce in the settlement to become a very large value. This will result in a mismatch between the nonces in the handler and the settlement contracts. 

A scenario:
 - Alice has never used the protocol before. She sends a token transfer message.
 - Her nonce in the handler contract becomes 1 and `txid` in the handler is computed by using `nonce = 1`.
 - Someone has increased her nonce in the settlement contract to `2` before her message was executed.
 - The settlement contract will compute its `txid` with `nonce = 2`. This `txid` will be send to the destination chain which will process the transaction and emit event to be used for the callback. The callback will use the `txid` with the inflated nonce and will pass it to [handler.receive_cross_chain_callback](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/settlement/contracts/ChakraSettlement.sol#L319).

 - Then, [this check](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/solidity/handler/contracts/ChakraSettlementHandler.sol#L378-L381) will revert because `nonce = 2` is not `Pending`.

In result the callbacks will never be executed.

The same is true for the Cairo version of the project, there the `tx_count` is not event related to the user. 

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-chakra/blob/abef77d95866f2fec93270491fc5abc9ab14f86d/cairo/settlement/src/settlement.cairo#L291

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider fetching the nonce from the settlement contract instead of tracking two nonces.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L509-L574
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L530-L531


# Vulnerability details

 
## Description 

The `CDPVault` contract is designed to manage collateralized debt positions, allowing users to deposit collateral, borrow against it, and handle liquidations. The [`liquidatePosition()` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L509-L574) is responsible for liquidating unsafe positions by repaying debt and releasing collateral. However, there is a critical issue in the calculation of `deltaDebt` and `penalty` within this function.

The `deltaDebt` is intended to represent the amount of debt to be repaid, while the `penalty` is a fee applied during liquidation. The current implementation incorrectly calculates `deltaDebt` using the `liquidationPenalty` parameter, which should instead be used solely for calculating the penalty. This miscalculation can lead to incorrect debt repayment and collateral release, causing financial discrepancies.

> Specifically, the code snippet:
[CDPVault.sol#L530-L531](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L530-L531)
```solidity
File: CDPVault.sol
530:         uint256 deltaDebt = wmul(repayAmount, liqConfig_.liquidationPenalty);
531:         uint256 penalty = wmul(repayAmount, WAD - liqConfig_.liquidationPenalty);
```
incorrectly calculates `deltaDebt` and `penalty`. The correct approach should be:
```solidity
uint256 deltaDebt = repayAmount;
uint256 penalty = wmul(repayAmount, liqConfig_.liquidationPenalty);
```

This ensures that `deltaDebt` accurately represents the debt to be repaid, and the `penalty` is correctly calculated based on the `liquidationPenalty`.

## Impact
Incorrect calculations during the liquidation process can lead to financial losses for the protocol and its users. Specifically, users may end up repaying incorrect amounts of debt or receiving incorrect amounts of collateral, undermining the financial integrity of the protocol. 

## Proof of Concept
1. **User** has a debt of 100 units and a liquidation penalty of 10%.
2. **User** triggers the `liquidatePosition()` function with a `repayAmount` of 100 units.
3. **Current Code** calculates `deltaDebt` as 10 units (incorrect) and `penalty` as 90 units (incorrect).
4. **Correct Code** should calculate `deltaDebt` as 100 units (correct) and `penalty` as 10 units (correct).
5. The incorrect calculation leads to the user repaying only 10 units of debt instead of 100, causing financial discrepancies.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update the `liquidatePosition()` function to correctly calculate `deltaDebt` and `penalty` as follows:

```solidity
function liquidatePosition(address owner, uint256 repayAmount) external whenNotPaused {
    // ... existing code ...

    // compute collateral to take, debt to repay and penalty to pay
    uint256 takeCollateral = wdiv(repayAmount, discountedPrice);
    uint256 deltaDebt = repayAmount; // Correctly represent the amount of debt to be repaid
    uint256 penalty = wmul(repayAmount, liqConfig_.liquidationPenalty); // Correctly calculate the penalty
    if (takeCollateral > position.collateral) revert CDPVault__tooHighRepayAmount();

    // ... existing code ...
}
```

This fix ensures that the liquidation process correctly handles the calculation of debt repayment and penalties, maintaining the financial integrity of the protocol.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/oracle/BalancerOracle.sol#L114-L136


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The protocol uses the `totalSupply()` function to obtain the number of LP tokens in a Balancer weighted pool. However, this function does not always return the correct count, and the [Balancer documentation](https://docs.balancer.fi/concepts/advanced/valuing-bpt/valuing-bpt.html#getting-bpt-supply) recommends using `getActualSupply()` instead.

Impact is a high one since the calculation of Weighted Pool Token Price is very important for the protocol, and any miscalculations could hurt the protocol and the users a lot. Most recent pools used will return wrong pool token price.


## Proof of Concept

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/oracle/BalancerOracle.sol#L114-L136

```solidity
 function update() external virtual onlyRole(KEEPER_ROLE) returns (uint256 safePrice_) {
        if (block.timestamp - lastUpdate < updateWaitWindow) revert BalancerOracle__update_InUpdateWaitWindow();
        // update the safe price first
        safePrice = safePrice_ = currentPrice;
        lastUpdate = block.timestamp;

        uint256[] memory weights = IWeightedPool(pool).getNormalizedWeights();
        uint256 totalSupply = IWeightedPool(pool).totalSupply();    <-------@

        uint256 totalPi = WAD;
        uint256[] memory prices = new uint256[](weights.length);
        // update balances in 18 decimals
        for (uint256 i = 0; i < weights.length; i++) {
            // reverts if the price is invalid or stale
            prices[i] = _getTokenPrice(i);
            uint256 val = wdiv(prices[i], weights[i]);
            uint256 indivPi = uint256(wpow(int256(val), int256(weights[i])));

            totalPi = wmul(totalPi, indivPi);
        }

        currentPrice = wdiv(wmul(totalPi, IWeightedPool(pool).getInvariant()), totalSupply);
    }
```

As seen above, `BalancerOracle::update()` which is used specifically for weighted balancer pools wrongly uses `totalSupply` all the time to get the total supply of the pool, but this would not be true for newer weighted pools.

Balancer pools have different methods to get their total supply of minted LP tokens, which is also specified in the balancer documentation.

Reference link: https://docs.balancer.fi/concepts/advanced/valuing-bpt/valuing-bpt.html#getting-bpt-supply

The documentation states that `totalSupply` is only used for older stable and weighted pools, and should not be used without checking it first.

>totalSupply
>In general, totalSupply only makes sense to call for older "legacy" pools. The original Weighted and Stable Pools do not have >pre-minted BPT, so they follow the typical convention of using totalSupply to account for issued pool shares

since the newer pools have pre-minted BPT and getActualSupply should be used in that case.

>getActualSupply
>This is the most common/current function to call. getActualSupply is used by the most recent versions of Weighted and Stable >Pools. It accounts for pre-minted BPT as well as due protocol fees.

Let's look at the `getActualSupply()` function code,


```solidity
    /**
     * @notice Returns the effective BPT supply.
     *
     * @dev This would be the same as `totalSupply` however the Pool owes debt to the Protocol in the form of unminted
     * BPT, which will be minted immediately before the next join or exit. We need to take these into account since,
     * even if they don't yet exist, they will effectively be included in any Pool operation that involves BPT.
     *
     * In the vast majority of cases, this function should be used instead of `totalSupply()`.
     *
     * **IMPORTANT NOTE**: calling this function within a Vault context (i.e. in the middle of a join or an exit) is
     * potentially unsafe, since the returned value is manipulable. It is up to the caller to ensure safety.
     *
     * This is because this function calculates the invariant, which requires the state of the pool to be in sync
     * with the state of the Vault. That condition may not be true in the middle of a join or an exit.
     *
     * To call this function safely, attempt to trigger the reentrancy guard in the Vault by calling a non-reentrant
     * function before calling `getActualSupply`. That will make the transaction revert in an unsafe context.
     * (See `whenNotInVaultContext` in `WeightedPool`).
     *
     * See https://forum.balancer.fi/t/reentrancy-vulnerability-scope-expanded/4345 for reference.
     */
    function getActualSupply() external view returns (uint256) {
        uint256 supply = totalSupply();

        (uint256 protocolFeesToBeMinted, ) = _getPreJoinExitProtocolFees(
            getInvariant(),
            _getNormalizedWeights(),
            supply
        );

        return supply.add(protocolFeesToBeMinted);
    }
```

As seen in `getActualSupply()` function comment above, it is apparent that `getActualSupply()` function should be used because the pool owes debt to the Protocol in the form of unminted BPT, which should be taken into consideration.

Newer Weighted Pools have `getActualSupply()` method when fees are paid in BPT inflation.

Most of the time, the assumption would be that only the new composable stable and weighted pools uses the `getActualSupply`, but that is not the case, since even the newer weighted pools have and uses the `getActualSupply`.

Let's have a look at below examples of newer weighted pools that uses `getActualSupply`

1. https://etherscan.io/address/0x9f9d900462492d4c21e9523ca95a7cd86142f298
2. https://etherscan.io/address/0x3ff3a210e57cfe679d9ad1e9ba6453a716c56a2e
3. https://etherscan.io/address/0xcf7b51ce5755513d4be016b0e28d6edeffa1d52a

The last one also being on Aura finance. Because of that, the interaction with newer weighted pools and also the future weighted pools would not be accurate since the wrong total supply is used and calculations like update() will return the incorrect/inaccurate price, which would hurt the protocol and the users.


## Tools used
- Manual review
- Reference:
This issue is very much referenced from https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2023-10-notional-judging/issues/36 issue which was found in Notional audit at Sherlock by Vagner.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Since the protocol would want to interact with multiple weighted pools, try to check first if the weighted pool you are interacting with is a newer one and uses the `getActualSupply` or if it is an older one and uses `totalSupply`, in that way the protocol could interact with multiple pools in the long run.

 [L-02] Min-max answer not checked in ChainlinkOracle.sol
Chainlink aggregators have a built in circuit breaker if the price of an asset goes outside of a predetermined price band. The result is that if an asset experiences a huge drop in value (i.e. LUNA crash) the price of the oracle will continue to return the minPrice instead of the actual price of the asset. ChainlinkFeedRegistry#latestRoundData pulls the associated aggregator and requests round data from it. ChainlinkAggregators have minPrice and maxPrice circuit breakers built into them. This means that if the price of the asset drops below the minPrice, the protocol will continue to value the token at minPrice instead of it’s actual value. This will allow users to take out huge amounts of bad debt and bankrupt the protocol.

Example: TokenA has a minPrice of $1. The price of TokenA drops to $0.10. The aggregator still returns $1 allowing the user to borrow against TokenA as if it is $1 which is 10x it’s actual value.

ChainlinkAdapterOracle should check the returned answer against the minPrice/maxPrice and revert if the answer is outside of the bounds:

    (, int256 answer, , uint256 updatedAt, ) = registry.latestRoundData(
        token,
        USD
    );
+   if (answer >= maxPrice or answer <= minPrice) revert();

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details 
Chainlink aggregators have a built-in circuit breaker if the price of an asset goes outside of a predetermined price band. The result is that if an asset experiences a huge drop in value (i.e. LUNA crash) the price of the oracle will continue to return the minPrice instead of the actual price of the asset.

This would allow user to continue borrowing with the asset but at the wrong price, which will lead to draining of the protocol. This is exactly what happened to [Venus](https://rekt.news/venus-blizz-rekt/) on BSC when LUNA imploded. However, the protocol missed to implement such a check.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The current implementation of the BalancerOracle is vulnerable to sandwich attacks, allowing malicious actors to manipulate the reported price. This can lead to severe consequences in the protocol that rely on this oracle for pricing, including:

1. Incorrect liquidations: Positions may be liquidated prematurely or not liquidated when they should be.
2. Mispriced loans: Users could borrow more or less than they should be able to based on their collateral.
3. Arbitrage opportunities: Attackers could profit from the price discrepancies between the manipulated oracle price and the actual market price.

The vulnerability could potentially lead to large-scale theft of funds or protocol insolvency in extreme cases.

## Proof of Concept

The vulnerability stems from the BalancerOracle's `update()` function, which calculates the current price based on the pool's state at a single point in time, making it susceptible to manipulation.

[function update()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/oracle/BalancerOracle.sol#L114-L116)
```Solidity
    function update() external virtual onlyRole(KEEPER_ROLE) returns (uint256 safePrice_) {
        if (block.timestamp - lastUpdate < updateWaitWindow) revert BalancerOracle__update_InUpdateWaitWindow();
```


Here's a proof of concept attack scenario:
**Let's assume;**
   - Balancer Weighted Pool: 1000 wETH (50% weight) and 2,000,000 USDC (50% weight)
   - Pool Invariant: 1,414,213,562
   - Total Supply of BPT: 1,000,000
   - Oracle Price: 2000 USDC per wETH (interpreted)

**Attacker actions:**
   a. Monitor the mempool for incoming "update" transactions to the BalancerOracle.
   b. Front-run the update by swapping 500 wETH for USDC, changing the pool composition to approximately 1500 wETH and 1,333,333 USDC.
   c. Allow the oracle update to execute, which will now report a BPT price of 1,414.21.
   d. Back-run by swapping USDC back to wETH, returning the pool to its original state.

**Result:**
   - The oracle now reports a BPT price of 1,414.21, which could be misinterpreted as 1 wETH = 1,414.21 USDC.
   - The actual market price remains close to 2000 USDC per wETH.
   - If a lending protocol uses this oracle, the attacker could now borrow against their wETH at the manipulated lower price, effectively borrowing more than they should be able to.
   - Alternatively, existing loans that should be liquidated might not be, allowing borrowers to avoid liquidation.

This attack can be repeated and scaled up, potentially leading to significant profit for the attacker and losses for the protocol and its users.

## Tools Used
Manual analysis

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

- Implement Time-Weighted Average Price (TWAP):
   Instead of using the current pool state, calculate the price based on a time-weighted average over a specific period. This makes it much more costly and difficult for attackers to manipulate the price.

- Implement price deviation checks:
   Add logic to detect and potentially revert significant price changes between updates. This can help prevent sudden, manipulated price swings from being reported.

- Add a delay mechanism:
   Implement a delay between price updates and their use in the protocol. This gives time for the pool state to stabilize and makes sandwich attacks less effective.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact  
Function `PendleConnector._getPositionTVL()` will revert unexpectedly, subsequently causing functions `TVLHelper.getTVL()` and `AccountingManager.TVL()` to revert, which causes DOS for the users same-block transactions such as deposits, withdraws, recording profit, or adjusting the profit.  
## Proof of Concept  
`PendleConnector._getPositionTVL()` relies on `PendleLpOracleLib.getLpToAssetRate()` and `PendlePtOracleLib.getPtToAssetRate()`. Downstream, the functions rely on `PendlePtOracleLib._getMarketLnImpliedRate()` which makes a call to `PendleMarketV3.observe()` with a duration hardcoded to 10 [code snippet 1](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/connectors/PendleConnector.sol#L271-L275),[code snippet 2](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/external/libraries/Pendle/PendlePtOracleLib.sol#L32). 

The observations in `PendleMarketV3` are updated every time there is a `PendleMarketV3._writeState()` call, for example, on a `PendleMarketV3.mint()` call, `PendleMarketV3.burn()` call, `PendleMarketV3.swapExactPtForSy()` call, or a `PendleMarketV3.swapSyForExactPt()` call. 

The issue is that if in the same block, after the `PendleMarketV3._writeState()` operation, there is a call to `PendleMarketV3.observe()` it will revert with `OracleTargetTooOld` - [reverting line snippet](https://github.com/pendle-finance/pendle-core-v2-public/blob/e48767be54fd668c4ea693ac56d13186f2517e3d/contracts/core/Market/OracleLib.sol#L136). Such a revert will then cause `TVLHelper.getTVL()` to revert and subsequently `TVL()` to revert when it is called to process deposits, withdrawals, or fee requests in `AccountingManager`. 

The `PendleMarketV3.observe()` revert will happen in blocks where any previous transaction (within the block), regardless if originating from a Vault Connector or an outside user of the Pendle Market, updates the observations in the Market through a `mint()`, `burn()`, `swapExactPtForSy()` or `swapSyForExactPt()` transaction. In Pendle Markets where the trade volume is high, this would mean a continuous DOS for the `AccountingManager` of a Vault that has a `PendleConnector` attached.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/helpers/valueOracle/NoyaValueOracle.sol#L89


# Vulnerability details

The `NoyaValueOracle` can define and execute different routes to obtain the price of each asset based on another by utilizing the `priceRoutes` mapping. For example, if we need the price of token A based on token C but lack a direct price source between A and C, the maintainer can define a route A -> B -> C, where there are price sources for the A and B pair and the B and C pair.

The core logic of this feature is present in the `NoyaValueOracle._getValue` function.
```solidity
function _getValue(address asset, address baseToken, uint256 amount, address[] memory sources)
    internal
    view
    returns (uint256 value)
{
    uint256 initialValue = amount;
    address quotingToken = asset;
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < sources.length; i++) {
        initialValue = _getValue(asset, sources[i], initialValue);
        quotingToken = sources[i];
    }
    return _getValue(quotingToken, baseToken, initialValue);
}
```
The issue arises from the fact that the current implementation uses `asset` instead of `quotingToken` in this line:
```solidity
initialValue = _getValue(asset, sources[i], initialValue);
```
It means that if we have a price route A -> B -> C -> D, where A is the `asset` and D is the `baseToken`, we would have the following simplified execution trace:
```
Before the loop:
initialValue = amount
quotingToken = A
First iteration:
initialValue = amount * price_a_b
quotingToken = B
Second iteration:
initialValue = (amount * price_a_b) * price_a_c <--- Here the calculation goes wrong
quotingToken = C
Return statement:
returnValue = ((amount * price_a_b) * price_a_c) * price_c_d
```
It can be seen that we use the wrong pair A and C on the second iteration instead of the correct pair B and C. If there is no registered price source for this pair, the execution just reverts. However, if the price source exists, instead of returning `((amount * price_a_b) * price_B_c) * price_c_d`, the current implementation returns `((amount * price_a_b) * price_A_c) * price_c_d`, which might differ significantly.

## Impact
This issue leads to incorrect calculation of token value, which significantly impacts the entire protocol, as the accuracy of this oracle contract is fundamental to the protocol's functioning.

## Proof of Concept
\-

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Replace `asset` with the `quotingToken` in this line of the `_getValue` function:
```solidity
-initialValue = _getValue(asset, sources[i], initialValue);
+initialValue = _getValue(quotingToken, sources[i], initialValue);
```

# Vulnerability details

# **Vulnerability Detail**

When the price of an asset deviates significantly from a predefined price range, Chainlink aggregators activate a circuit breaker mechanism. In situations like the crash of LUNA, this mechanism causes the oracle to consistently return the minimum price instead of the actual price of the asset. Consequently, users can continue to borrow against the asset, but at an incorrect price. This scenario occurred on Venus on the Binance Smart Chain (BSC) during the collapse of LUNA.

The ChainLink Oracle Connector doesn’t implement any checks to handle such scenarios.

# **Proof of Concept**

The ChainlinkFeedRegistry#latestRoundData function retrieves round data from the associated aggregator. These Chainlink aggregators include circuit breakers for minPrice and maxPrice, ensuring that if the asset's price falls below the minPrice, the protocol will continue to value the token at minPrice rather than its actual value. This scenario enables users to borrow significant amounts of bad debt, potentially leading to bankruptcy for the protocol.

For instance, consider TokenA with a minPrice set at $1. If the price of TokenA drops to $0.10, the aggregator still reports $1

# **Impact**

The chainlink could return incorrect prices.

# **Recommendation**

ChainlinkAdapterOracle should check the returned answer against the minPrice/maxPrice and revert if the answer is outside of the bounds:

```solidity
    (, int256 answer, , uint256 updatedAt, ) = registry.latestRoundData(
        token,
        USD
    );
+   if (answer >= maxPrice or answer <= minPrice) revert();
```

The function will revert and will not return the value.

It is not the best variant to set it to 24 hours, but it will eliminate the risk of revert, and compare the risk of returning the outdated data, i suppose this option is worth to take into account.

# Vulnerability details




## Impact
`totalAssets()` may revert, which in turn causes `convertToShares()` and `convertToAssets()` to revert, each possibility of revert of which is a violation ERC-4626.

## Proof of Concept
[AccountingManager is to be ERC-4626 compliant](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya?tab=readme-ov-file#:~:text=src/accountingManager/AccountingManager,ERC4626). Therefore [`totalAssets()` MUST NOT revert](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626#:~:text=in%20the%20Vault.-,MUST%20NOT%20revert.,-%2D%20name%3A).

However, `AccountingManager.totalAssets()` [returns `TVL()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/accountingManager/AccountingManager.sol#L592) which [returns a sum including `TVLHelper.getTVL()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/accountingManager/AccountingManager.sol#L628) which [calls `IConnector.getPositionTVL()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/helpers/TVLHelper.sol#L22) on the connector of every position. In all connectors this calls `NoyaValueOracle._getValue()` which [explicitly may revert](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/helpers/valueOracle/NoyaValueOracle.sol#L107) if an oracle is unavailable. `AccountingManager.totalAssets()` may thus revert.

This then also causes `convertToShares()` and `convertToAssets()`, which make use of `totalAssets()` to revert.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider returning `0` instead of reverting. If an oracle is unavailable it seems reasonable to consider this asset temporarily worthless. This might cause a price drop in `totalAssets()` instead of reverting. Consider what the implications of this could be, if any. If necessary consider perhaps using the last known value as an "oracle" of last resort instead of reverting.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/accountingManager/Registry.sol#L32


# Vulnerability details

The Registry is a critical part of the protocol. It's primary responsibility is storing information related to the vaults and the positions. It does this by exposing functionality for authorized roles to add vaults and connectors, as well as update trusted tokens and trusted positions. 

It is a core invariant of the system that functionality should be accessible by an individual possessing the correct trusted roles.

The system attempts to enforce this invariant through access modifiers. The issues is that the logic of the onlyVaultMaintainer modifier in Registry.sol is flawed such that any user authorized as a vault maintainer that attempts to call a function with the onlyVaultMaintainer modifer will fail with revert reason UnauthorizedAccess.

[PositionRegistry::onlyVaultMaintainer](
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/accountingManager/Registry.sol#L32)

```solidity
    modifier onlyVaultMaintainer(uint256 _vaultId) {
        if (msg.sender != vaults[_vaultId].maintainer || hasRole(EMERGENCY_ROLE, msg.sender) == false) {
            revert UnauthorizedAccess();
        }
        _;
    }
```


Consider the following outcomes of the modifier condition (with OR):
-  Neither Role - T || T == T 
     - Result: (Revert) [Correct]
-  Both Roles -  F || F = F 
    - (No Revert) [Correct*  because user has maintainer]
-  Maintainer but not Emergency - F || T = T 
    - (Revert) [INCORRECT - violates the spirit of the modifier]
-  Emergency but not Maintainer - T || F = T 
    - (Revert) [Correct] 

Based on the flawed logic a user would need to have both the MAINTAINER_ROLE for the vault as well as the EMERGENCY_ROLE in order for the system to allow them to successfully call functions that have the onlyVaultMaintainer modifier applied. 

The [All trusted roles in the protocol](https://code4rena.com/audits/2024-04-noya) section on the contest page describes the emergency role as `"a cold wallet that is going to be used in situations that a position is stuck or another role of noya is compromised."`

Granting the EMERGENCY_ROLE to the vault maintainers is not the normal and intended configuration for the system. Thus it's reasonable to assume that functions using the onlyVaultMaintainer modifier for access control would be effectively inaccessible if the system was deployed as is. Making them accessible would mean putting the system in an unintended and unreasonable configuration. 


## Impact

The direct impact is that the [addConnector](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/accountingManager/Registry.sol#L188), [updateConnectorTrustedTokens](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/accountingManager/Registry.sol#L207), and [removeTrustedPosition](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/accountingManager/Registry.sol#L266), functions of PositionRegistry become inaccessible / unusable. 

The indirect impacts of this are far reaching. While `addVault()` is technically accessible because it directly uses the OpenZeppelin `onlyRole(MAINTAINER_ROLE)` modifier to enforce access control. The loss of ability to add connectors leaves any added vaults in a limited and non-useful state. 

`addTrustedPosition` - this functionality is lost even without using onlyVaultMaintainer modifier because it relies on a Calculator Connector being added and enabled [or else it reverts](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/accountingManager/Registry.sol#L251), but without addConnector the Calculator Connector cannot be added.

`updateHoldingPosition` - this functionality is lost because it relies on Trusted Positions which can't be added without connectors. 

Essentially loss of ability to add connectors lead to loss of most useful Registry functionality. The system cannot work properly without the registry and thus the protocol becomes unusable when compared to the original intention and vision. 

## Proof of Concept

Test setup 
 * clone https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya
* Open the testStarter.sol in the protocol's existing test suite (testFoundry/utils/testStarter.sol)
* Modify [line 42 of deployEverythingNormal](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/testFoundry/utils/testStarter.sol#L42 ) function so that the Registry isn't deployed using the same address for Governor, Maintainer, and Emergency. It's enough to change the Emergency address below to something like address(123). 
    * The test suite understandably set owner as all the roles for convenience but this prevented detection of the flawed modifier logic.

```solidity

    function deployEverythingNormal(address _base) public {
        baseToken = _base;
        address distinctEmergencyAddr = address(123);
        // registry = new PositionRegistry(owner, owner, owner, address(0));
        // Above is original approach, below is modification to expose flawed logic
        registry = new PositionRegistry(owner, owner, distinctEmergencyAddr, address(0));
        console.log("PositionRegistry deployed: %s", address(registry));
        deployNoyaOracle();

        deployChainlinkOracle();
        deployNoyaAccounting();
       
       ...
       ...
}
```

*  Execute: `forge test`
    * Most registry logic will become unusable by the maintainer without unreasonably granting them the EMERGENCY_ROLE. This disrupts normal functioning related to vaults, connectors, trusted tokens, and trusted positions sufficiently to consider the protocol unusable as originally intended.  This clearly seen as trying to remove use of the impacted registry logic or work around it will cause the entire protocol test suite to fail. 


## Tools Used

* Manual review
* Foundry


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The modifier will work correctly if the`== false` is removed from the side side of the condition ( `hasRole(EMERGENCY_ROLE, msg.sender) == false)` ) as seen below.


```solidity
    modifier onlyVaultMaintainer(uint256 _vaultId) {
        if (msg.sender != vaults[_vaultId].maintainer || hasRole(EMERGENCY_ROLE, msg.sender)) {
            revert UnauthorizedAccess();
        }
        _;
    }
```

With this change the outcomes of the modifier condition become:
-  Neither Role - T || F == T 
     - Result: (Revert) [Correct]
-  Both Roles -  F || T = T 
    - Result: (Revert) [Correct]
-  Maintainer but not Emergency - F || F = F 
    - (No Revert) [Correct]
-  Emergency but not Maintainer - T || T = T 
    - (Revert) [Correct] 


Lastly its important the re-iterate that this bug would have be caught by the protocol testing suite if it had been configured in a more realistic way in this case by using distinct addresses for distinct roles in the testing setup.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/connectors/AaveConnector.sol#L116


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

When calculating the TVL of a position held the AaveConnector, in case the debt of a position is higher than the collateral value the function call to `_getPositionTVL` will revert because of underflow. If this is the case, the deposit and withdraw process of the corresponding vault which need this function to pass will be DoSed and all user funds will be locked.


## Proof of Concept
In the Aave protocol users/vaults can borrow tokens by depositing collateral to Aave and borrowing against this collateral. If the health factor of the account falls below Aave`s minimum health factor, the account can be liquidated. 

A liquidator can repay [a part or all debt]( https://docs.aave.com/developers/guides/liquidations) of the account and get the corresponding collateral plus an additional bonus (liquidation bonus) for his work. In turbulent market conditions when demand for transactions is high and prices of collateral fall fast, the gas cost for liquidations can become higher than the `liquidation bonus` a liquidator would get making it unprofitable to liquidate a position. This can result in an account having more debt than assets.

The issue with the current implementation of the Aave connector lays in the function `_getPositionTVL` that is used to calculate the TVL of an position held by the AaveConnector. 

This function gets the value of the collateral (totalCollateralBase) and the debt (totalDebtBase) of the connector and then deducts the debt value from the collateral value:


```java
        (uint256 totalCollateralBase, uint256 totalDebtBase,,,,) = IPool(pool).getUserAccountData(address(this));
        uint256 poolBaseAmount = totalCollateralBase - totalDebtBase; 
```
As described above, an account can have more debt than collateral resulting in an underflow when calculating the return value and therefor in a revert of any call to the `_getPositionTVL`.

This will lead to a DOS for processing any deposits and withdrawals of the associated vault, locking all assets of the users in the vault.
 


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add a check to the `_getPositionTVL` function which ensures that the value of the collateral is bigger than the debt value. If this is not the case, return 0. This is also ok from a global TVL standpoint since it does not make economic sense to repay a debt position where the collateral which the vault gets back is worth less than the repayment value.

```dif
+	if(totalCollateralBase < totalDebtBase) return 0;
       	uint256 poolBaseAmount = totalCollateralBase - totalDebtBase;
       	return valueOracle.getValue(poolBaseToken, base, poolBaseAmount); 
```

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details

Note about contest scope: `Oracle::transform` is being called from `KatanaV3Pool::_modifyPosition()` and `KatanaV3Pool::swap()` (line 308, line 693 in KatanaV3Pool.sol), and the KatanaV3Pool contract is in scope of this contest.

The function `Oracle::transform()` is used to update observations of the pool state over time, which are critical for accurate price feeds, liquidity calculations, and potentially reward distributions. However, there is an issue with the handling of the `liquidity` parameter when it is 0.

The current implementation uses a ternary operator to avoid division by zero, but this approach can lead to inaccurate accumulation of secondsPerLiquidityCumulativeX128 when the pool has no liquidity (line 40 katana-v3-contracts/src/core/libraries/Oracle.sol):

```solidity
+ ((uint160(delta) << 128) / (liquidity > 0 ? liquidity : 1)),
```

With 0 liquidity it is dividing by 1 instead of zero to avoid reverting, but this introduces a logical error in the calculations.

## Impact

Overestimation of time-weighted average liquidity:
During periods of zero liquidity, the function is still accumulating time as if there was 1 unit of liquidity.

Misleading Oracle Data: Any system relying on this oracle for liquidity data will receive inaccurate information. This could affect trading decisions, risk assessments, or any other mechanisms that depend on accurate liquidity reporting.

## Example

We have a pool that alternates between having liquidity and being empty:

T0: Liquidity = 1000

T100: Liquidity drops to 0

T200: Liquidity increases to 2000

T300: Observation is taken

With our current implementation:

From T0 to T100 and from T200 to T300 we accumulate 100 seconds worth of liquidity.

However from T100 to T200, we incorrectly accumulate 100 seconds as if there was 1 unit of liquidity.

This results in an overestimation of the average liquidity over this period.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Modify `Oracle::transform()` in order to skip accumulation if `liquidity` is 0, so that `secondsPerLiquidityCumulativeX128` is only accumulated if there is liquidity in the pool.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/OwnershipNFTs.sol#L98-L107


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The vulnerability arises from the fact that after a token transfer, the approval status for the token is not revoked. Specifically, the `getApproved[_tokenId]` is not updated on transfer.
This allows the previous owner (or any approved address) to reclaim the NFT by using the approval mechanism to re-transfer the token back to themselves. This is critical because the new owner of the NFT may lose their asset without realizing it, leading to potential exploitation, loss of assets, and decreased trust in the platform.

## Details
In the provided `approve` function, any user can approve themselves or another address for a specific token ID:

```solidity
/// @inheritdoc IERC721Metadata
function approve(address _approved, uint256 _tokenId) external payable {
    _requireAuthorised(msg.sender, _tokenId);
    getApproved[_tokenId] = _approved;
}
```

Since the approval is not revoked upon transfer, the previous owner retains the ability to re-transfer the NFT. The `_requireAuthorised` function is the only check on transfer permission:

```solidity
function _requireAuthorised(address _from, uint256 _tokenId) internal view {
    // revert if the sender is not authorised or the owner
    bool isAllowed =
        msg.sender == _from ||
        isApprovedForAll[_from][msg.sender] ||
        msg.sender == getApproved[_tokenId];

    require(isAllowed, "not allowed");
    require(ownerOf(_tokenId) == _from, "_from is not the owner!");
}
```

### Step-by-Step PoC:
1. **Initial Approval**: The owner of a token (`owner1`) approves an address (`addr2`) to transfer their token.
2. **Token Transfer**: The token is transferred from `owner1` to `newOwner`.
3. **Approval Not Revoked**: The approval for `addr2` is not revoked after the transfer.
4. **NFT Recovery**: `addr2` can still use their approval to transfer the NFT back to themselves, effectively recovering the NFT from `newOwner`.

Note to the judge: there is no existing tests for this specific smart contract (because it is in solidity). A coded POC for this easy-to-understand vulnerability would involve to create all deployment logic.

## Tools Used
Manual code review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To prevent this vulnerability, any existing approvals should be revoked when a token is transferred. This can be achieved by adding a line in the transfer function to clear the approval:

```solidity
getApproved[_tokenId] = address(0);
```

This line should be added to the token transfer function to ensure that any previously approved addresses cannot transfer the NFT after it has been sold or transferred to a new owner.

# Vulnerability details

## Summary

Do Note that this vulnerability was highly inspired by this recent finding -
- https://mirror.xyz/verbsteam.eth/TP917T6vm6gXuVAxbQ34ZCn7dNiHabu3UW-ninwalVc.

The `StRSRVotes` contract contains a similar vulnerability to the one described in the Nouns NFT scenario. The issue lies in the `_moveVotingPower` function, which is called during token transfers and delegations.

We have identified a critical vulnerability in the `StRSRP1Votes` contract. When `delegateBySig` is called, potential delegation to the zero address can lead to permanent loss of the user's voting power.

Users are no longer able to participate in the voting decisions When this function is used to delegate to address zero, the delegator wallet loses all its voting power and can no longer transfer their votes out of that wallet.


## Vulnerability Details

The` _moveVotingPower` function allows delegation to address(0), which can lead to permanent loss of voting power. 

The issue occurs when an `StRSR` owner delegates their voting power to an EOA. If the delegate, whether intentionally or unintentionally, uses the `delegateBySig` function to delegate to the zero address, one unit of voting power is permanently burned. This results in the associated losing its voting power and becoming non-transferrable. The transfer attempt will revert due to an underflow error when the contract attempts to reduce the sender's already zero voting power. When delegating to `address(0)`, voting power is subtracted from the source but not added to any destination, effectively burning it.

The `_afterTokenTransfer` function calls `_moveVotingPower`, potentially causing issues during transfers if a user's voting power has been compromised. The `stakeAndDelegate` function allows users to stake and delegate in one transaction, potentially exacerbating the issue if misused.

- Who's at risk? `StRSR` token holders delegating to EOA accounts.
- What's the damage? `StRSR` tokens can become non-transferrable with lost voting power.
- How likely is it to happen? Low probability if delegates are trusted not to transfer to a zero address, but mistakes do happen. And it can also be perfomed by a malicious actor.


## Impact:

Voting Power Loss: The affected user loses its voting power permanently, reducing its utility in governance processes.



## Proof of Concept:

1.  Setup:
        Alice owns `StRSR` 1.
        Bob owns `StRSR` 2.

2.  Delegation:
        Alice delegates her voting power to Bob (Alice votes: 0; Bob votes: 2).

3.  Faulty Delegation:
        Bob uses `delegateBySig` to delegate his voting power to the zero address (0x0000...).
        One vote is permanently burned (Alice votes: 0; Bob votes: 1).

4.  Transfer:
        Bob transfers `StRSR` 2 to a new wallet, Bobby (Alice votes: 0; Bob votes: 0; Bobby votes: 1).

5.  Zombie Noun:
        Alice's `StRSR` 1 becomes a zombie: it has no voting power and cannot be transferred out of Alice's wallet due to an underflow error.
    
    
Root Cause:
The root cause lies in the StRSRP1Votes contract's _moveDelegates function, which handles vote delegation and transfer operations. The function fails to account for the scenario where voting power is delegated to the zero address. Specifically, when delegateBySig is used to delegate to the zero address, the function deducts voting power from the sender but does not reassign it to any recipient, leading to an irrecoverable loss of voting power. Additionally, this causes an underflow error during subsequent transfer attempts.



## Recommended Mitigation:

-  The `StRSRP1Votes` contract should be refactored to include checks that prevent delegation to the address (0x0000...).
        
- Reserve owners should delegate their voting power only to smart contract accounts, such as those created with Gnosis Safe, to prevent this vulnerability from being exploited.

## Description

The `GnosisTrade` contract facilitates trades using the Gnosis EasyAuction mechanism. The [`settle()` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-reserve/blob/3f133997e186465f4904553b0f8e86ecb7bbacbf/contracts/plugins/trading/GnosisTrade.sol#L175-L221) is responsible for finalizing the auction, transferring tokens, and verifying if the auction's clearing price meets the expected worst-case price. However, there is a vulnerability in the way the clearing price is calculated and compared to the worst-case price, potentially allowing an attacker to manipulate the auction outcome by exploiting rounding errors.

The [`settle()` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-reserve/blob/3f133997e186465f4904553b0f8e86ecb7bbacbf/contracts/plugins/trading/GnosisTrade.sol#L175-L221) includes the following logic to calculate the clearing price:

```solidity
File: GnosisTrade.sol
212:             // Gnosis rounds defensively in the buy token; we should not consider it a violation
213:             uint256 adjustedSoldAmt = Math.max(soldAmt, 1);
214:             uint256 adjustedBuyAmt = boughtAmt + 1;
215: 
216:             // D27{buyTok/sellTok}
217:             uint192 clearingPrice = shiftl_toFix(adjustedBuyAmt, 9).divu(adjustedSoldAmt, FLOOR);
218:             if (clearingPrice.lt(worstCasePrice)) broker.reportViolation();

```

The issue arises from two main factors:
1. The use of `Math.max(soldAmt, 1)` to ensure a non-zero denominator.
2. The addition of 1 to `boughtAmt` to account for Gnosis' defensive rounding.

These adjustments, combined with the `FLOOR` rounding in the `divu()` function, can lead to scenarios where an attacker can manipulate the auction to barely avoid triggering a violation report, even when the actual clearing price is below the worst-case price.

For example, if the `worstCasePrice` is set to 100 and an attacker manages to settle the auction with `soldAmt = 100` and `boughtAmt = 9900`, the actual price would be 99. However, due to the adjustments and rounding, the calculated `clearingPrice` would be 100, equal to the `worstCasePrice`, thus avoiding a violation report.

## Impact

Attackers can exploit the rounding mechanism to settle auctions at prices slightly below the worst-case price without triggering violation reports. 

Legitimate participants may receive fewer tokens than expected based on the intended worst-case price protection, resulting in direct financial losses. 


## Proof of Concept

1. Alice initiates an auction with a `worstCasePrice` of 100 (assuming appropriate scaling).
2. The auction proceeds, and Bob (the attacker) manipulates the final bid to result in:
   - `soldAmt = 100`
   - `boughtAmt = 9900` (which would normally result in a price of 99, below the worst-case price)
3. In the `settle()` function:
   - `adjustedSoldAmt` becomes 100 (due to `Math.max(soldAmt, 1)`)
   - `adjustedBuyAmt` becomes 9901 (due to `boughtAmt + 1`)
4. The `clearingPrice` calculation:
   ``
   clearingPrice = shiftl_toFix(9901, 9).divu(100, FLOOR);
   ``
   Due to rounding, this results in a `clearingPrice` of 100, equal to the `worstCasePrice`.
5. The condition `clearingPrice.lt(worstCasePrice)` evaluates to false, so no violation is reported.
6. The auction settles at an effective price of 99, below the worst-case price, without triggering a violation report.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To mitigate this vulnerability, implement a more robust comparison mechanism that accounts for potential rounding errors. Here's a proposed fix:

```diff
function settle()
    external
    stateTransition(TradeStatus.OPEN, TradeStatus.CLOSED)
    returns (uint256 soldAmt, uint256 boughtAmt)
{
    // ... existing code ...

    if (sellBal < initBal) {
        soldAmt = initBal - sellBal;

-       uint256 adjustedSoldAmt = Math.max(soldAmt, 1);
-       uint256 adjustedBuyAmt = boughtAmt + 1;
-       uint192 clearingPrice = shiftl_toFix(adjustedBuyAmt, 9).divu(adjustedSoldAmt, FLOOR);
-       if (clearingPrice.lt(worstCasePrice)) broker.reportViolation();

+       // Use precise calculations without adjustments
+       uint192 clearingPrice = shiftl_toFix(boughtAmt, 9).divu(soldAmt, CEIL);
+       if (clearingPrice.lte(worstCasePrice)) broker.reportViolation();
    }

    // ... rest of the function ...
}
```

This change does the following:
1. Removes the adjustments to `soldAmt` and `boughtAmt`, using the actual values.
2. Changes the rounding mode in `divu()` from `FLOOR` to `CEIL`, ensuring we err on the side of caution.
3. Changes the comparison from `lt` (less than) to `lte` (less than or equal to), to catch cases where the clearing price exactly matches the worst-case price.
